Mr. Speaker, I first wish to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for asserting and vindicating, in what he has said, a high parliamentary principle. There has been an exchange of ideas between the Prime Minister and myself which has led to the measure of agreement that he has accurately described in the remarks he has made. I think that this, Mr. Speaker, is parliament at its very best. We do welcome the unqualified assurance by the Prime Minister that an appropriate amendment will be introduced when we are in committee of the whole house to make the defence production department a permanent department of government, with appropriate administrative authority, and to place a limit of three years after the termination of the present Defence Production Act upon those special powers which have been under discussion in this long debate.
In addition to this vitally important amendment, the Prime Minister has referred to the amendment which was proposed by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) on June 13, and which would have the effect of bringing before the house a discussion of the orders in council or ministerial orders made under the provisions of this act when it becomes law. This assurance has been interpreted in the amendment which the Prime Minister has read, and which would become the amendment before the house when we are in committee.
It would provide that in addition to the publication in the Canada Gazette, the orders in council or ministerial orders under this act would be tabled forthwith and that there
Defence Production Act would be a procedure by which an early debate could be assured upon the petition of 10 members.	,
I would recall, Mr. Speaker, that at the time we indicated the proposal of the Minister of Defence Production did not, in itself, satisfy our demands for a time limit upon the special powers. I wish to emphasize further that we never suggested that this provision, in association with other appropriate amendments, could not satisfy a very useful purpose. On the contrary, we think it is a useful amendment to the act, and in combination with the amendment now proposed by the Prime Minister, could be very valuable indeed. While we would have preferred to see the whole act rewritten, I agree with the Prime Minister that we have discussed this in a realistic manner. We recognize that the government has the responsibility of introducing legislation. We are not forgetful of the fact that the government has a majority to support its position.
At all times since the motion to introduce this bill was placed before the house, we have sought to obtain certain results. The statement by the Prime Minister in regard to the amendment which will be placed before us in committee of the whole substantially meets all the demands that we have made. This amendment in fact, Mr. Speaker, alters vastly, totally and fundamentally the whole character of the amending bill now before us. There are some powers in section 15 which we do not like. In our discussion we have criticized the effect of these powers in combination with some of the other sections of the act falling within that group of special sections which now will have a time limit placed upon them. Nevertheless, we must recognize that, desirable or undesirable, those powers contained in section 15 are already contained in the Defence Supplies Act, which is still on the statute books and which would become operative again if the Defence Production Act came to an end.
We do not withdraw any argument we have made in this debate. Those arguments expressed our firm conviction that sweeping powers such as those contained in sections 23 to 31 should not be continuing powers in this or any other act. Between now and the time these sections come to an end under the amendment which the Prime Minister has read to the house, there will be ample opportunity to consider the whole act, and the parliamentary principles which we have asserted over these past few weeks. That in itself, Mr. Speaker, we regard as a satisfactory safeguard to the principles we have enunciated. Whether the next government be formed by the Liberal or by the Conservative

Defence Production Act party, that government will not be likely to forget that any attempt to disregard those principles would unquestionably produce a similar debate.
What we have been doing during these recent weeks is to prevent, if possible, by proper parliamentary procedure the passing of a bill to which we have the strongest objection, in the form in which it was presented. I can assure the house we were ready to continue that legitimate obstruction for some considerable time yet. In fact, the excellent attendance of our members today demonstrates how ready they were to continue this debate, and I can assure you that they were ready to proceed. That is now unnecessary; at least, I hope there will be an agreement among the members that it is unnecessary. The result we sought has been substantially achieved. It is, therefore, my hope that without further debate we can now proceed with second reading and in committee of the whole house adopt the amendment proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I would also hope that we could then approve of third reading this afternoon and bring this debate to an end.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to prolong an already lengthy debate. All I am going to say is, I am very happy indeed to know that a solution has been found to the controversy that has raged in the house over a considerable length of time. I have believed throughout that some time limit should be placed on the special powers in the bill. That has been achieved. If special powers are given I believe that the legislation containing them should come before the house from time to time for reconsideration. From the outset I have believed that the principle of the bill was sound. To continue the department was absolutely essential. To give these powers, subject to review at a subsequent date, was also essential because I am convinced that in the light of world conditions today it is necessary for the government of Canada to exercise a considerable amount of control whenever necessary over the raw materials needed in the national interests and also over industrial and other efforts in the interests of the nation.
Consequently the proposals made this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and accepted by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) are quite in line with my own thinking. I have not taken any particular part in the debate because, our position having been made clear at the resolution stage by our spokesman, I did not think, with the debate going on as it was, it was necessary to intervene with the exception of last week


when I felt we should make it very clear indeed that we were anxious to see the kind of compromise effected, if you can call it a compromise, that has been effected this afternoon. I join with the Leader of the Opposition in hoping that we may adopt second reading now, consider the bill and the amendments in committee, and at the earliest possible moment, in conformity with our usual consideration of procedures, give final approval to the bill, if possible, today.

Mr. Speaker, may I take a moment to express the gratification that I and my group feel that a common-sense solution has been found to what appeared to be a rather difficult impasse that has existed in the house for quite some time. I want to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the statement he made this afternoon and the assurance he gave that in committee the amendments he read to us will be embodied in the bill. Those amendments are entirely satisfactory to us. As a matter of fact they go somewhat beyond what I proposed in the house nearly a week ago as a satisfactory solution, I then believed, to the controversy that had raged for some days.
May I also take this opportunity to congratulate the opposition on what I thought was a good fight on a principle in which they believe and in which I believe. We stood with the opposition on that principle because we believed in it. We wanted to see the government have their Department of Defence Production made permanent, but at the same time we expressed at the beginning, and have continued to express right down to this time, our determination that there should be certain portions at least of the bill setting up the department made subject to some sort of reference to parliament periodically so that we would have control of those sections here. I congratulate the opposition on their good fight, one that has sustained a principle in which they believe and in which I believe, and has also gone far to establish and maintain the supremacy of parliament in which we also believe.
At the same time may I express sincere congratulations to the Prime Minister because I believe it takes considerable courage to face up to what the government has faced during the past two or three weeks. In my judgment it takes courage, and it also takes courage to come forward in a conciliatory spirit and yield to the overwhelming desire of parliament, as I have been able to size it up, to achieve this compromise and a settlement of what was a real controversy.
I congratulate him and I congratulate the government on seeing that we were determined to have a change in the bill. On the

assurance they have given us we will support second reading of the bill and we hope that we will be able to go through the committee stage and get third reading this afternoon.

speechtext: As the chairman has pointed out, there were some amendments to this bill in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. It might be helpful if the minister were to explain those amendments to the committee, and also let us know whether he has in mind making any further amendments at this stage. There are one or two points he agreed to consider, and perhaps he would make a statement now.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to respond to the invitation of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and try to give just a brief outline of the amendments which are proposed and which were discussed in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and which, as you pointed out, Mr. Chairman, are to be found at page 844 of Votes and Proceedings for Friday, July 1.
The first of these amendments adds to subsection 1 of section 32 words which are intended to have the effect of limiting agreed charges to the transport of goods from one point in Canada to another point in Canada. I may say, Mr. Chairman, that this language was agreed upon as best meeting the unanimous desire of members of the committee that agreed charges should apply only to transport in Canada, and not to other parts of the world.
When this amendment was proposed, I think it was hoped at that time that the language woud be sufficiently restrictive to meet the objections of certain non-conference
[Mr. Drew.)
shipping companies which felt that certain practices now carried on by the railroads discriminated against them, and so, by limiting in proper legal language the agreed charge to the transport of goods in Canada, the main objection which they had raised would be overcome.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the second amendment was not one of very great substance. Hon. members will recall that at present where an agreement for agreed charges is from or to a competitive point, or between competitive points, it is necessary for both railways to become parties to the agreed charge. The change in wording was to make possible the making of an agreed charge by one railway if the other railway which was not interested in carrying the kind of goods covered by the charge was agreeable to the charge being made.
The third amendment, Mr. Chairman, is merely a question of going back to the language used by Mr. Justice Turgeon in his report with regard to the cases where a carrier by water joins in the making of an agreed charge. There is no substantial difference between the language of the amendment and the original language of subclause 5 of the bill as introduced in this house.
The fourth amendment involves the replacement of clause 33 of the bill by a new clause 33 which I think, it will be found, makes only one substantial change in clause 33. In the bill as originally drafted there is a provision by which a carrier, or an association of carriers, either by water or by rail, or an association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality may, under certain conditions, complain to the Minister of Transport that an agreed charge is discriminatory or that it places the business of the complainant at an unfair disadvantage. In those conditions, the Minister of Transport is empowered in Bill No. 449 to refer the agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners for investigation.
During the course of the discussions before the standing committee representations were made by the Canadian Trucking Associations and, as I indicated a moment ago, by representatives of two non-conference shipping companies which, it seemed to me, made it desirable to broaden the conditions under which a particular agreed charge might be referred to the board of transport commissioners. The essence of the amendment which replaces the original clause 33 appears in subclause 2. It empowers the governor in council, if he has reason to believe that

an agreed charge is undesirable in the public interest, to refer that agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners for investigation.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the sum and substance of the amendments which are recommended by the committee. I think I should say that the effect of the amendment to clause 33 is that it opens the door wide to an agreed charge or to one or more agreed charges being referred to the board of transport commissioners whenever there are circumstances which would seem to justify an inquiry being made by the board into the agreed charge which is the subject of reference, or if there be more than one, to all of those covered by the reference. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this change puts into the bill the necessary amount of flexibility so that if, as I said in the committee, broadly speaking, the agreed charges are found to contain provisions which are discriminatory against any form of transportation, it will be possible, if the governor in council is of the opinion that the practice is undesirable in the public interest, to refer the agreed charges to the board so that it might investigate them.
It will be found that the amendment, just as the bill itself, enables the board upon a reference to cancel or vary the agreed charges referred to it.
During the course of our discussions a question was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra which perhaps I should attempt to deal with. As far as my memory serves me, this is the only item as to which I undertook to give further consideration. I should like to say to the committee that, after considering the matter fully, I do not think any further amendment ought to be made to the bill. I think that the point raised in committee has been adequately taken care of.
The point I refer to is the contention which was emphasized rather strongly by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, namely, that the agreed charge should by the statute itself be required to be compensatory. I promised the hon. member during the committee stage that I would reconsider the question of whether it could be definitely put into the bill or not. I came to the conclusion that not only was it adequately covered under the present legislation but that it would be practically impossible to amend the legislation by providing for a more direct reference of an agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners in order to determine whether it was compensatory or not. I feel perfectly sure that if hon. members reflect upon the matter they would agree that if we are to
Transport Act
make the agreed charge the effective instrument it should be, we cannot at the same time add further procedure which must be observed so that in effect by doing so we shall make the new procedure just as long, just as complicated and just as uncertain as the procedure followed at present.
As hon. members will perhaps recall, under the existing legislation the present practice is that when the agreed charge is arrived at between the carriers and a group of shippers, it must be submitted to the board of transport commissioners for its approval. One of the points which must be investigated at present is, what is the effect of the agreed charge on the net revenue of the carrier?
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have found that the necessity of submitting every agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners for its approval before it becomes effective is robbing the agreed charge of most of its efficacy as an instrument of competition. The main principle of Mr. Justice Turgeon's recommendation is that the procedure should be simplified so that the railways may be placed on what would be regarded by them as a more nearly equal basis of competition with the trucking industry. If we go back to the present requirement that the board must decide whether or not an agreed charge is compensatory I fear we shall be robbing the agreed charge of a great deal of its utility and usefulness as an element of competition. Consequently I do not think that I can accept any amendment which in fact is going to put the agreed charge in the strait-jacket it was in and which it still is in under the existing legislation.
I do not want hon. members to believe that the proposed legislation does not imply that the agreed charge must be compensatory. I know that the requirement of Bill No. 449 is not identical with the legislation which it replaces. I am not for an instant attempting to create in the minds of the members of this committee the impression that the two bills are identical from a legal point of view, but I do say that Bill No. 449, with the amendment to which I referred a moment ago, makes it abundantly clear that the agreed charge should be compensatory. If an agreed charge is referred to the board of transport commissioners one of the first things which they must inquire into is the effect that the making of the agreed charge is likely to have on the net revenues of the carrier who is a party to it. That is just as clear as the language of the existing statute and in my view it is perfectly clear that the principle of the legislation we are now discussing is that the agreed charge should be compensatory.

Transport Act
Let us suppose for a moment that the conditions which were imagined by some members of the committee came about and the railroads, because they were seemingly not under any direct legal prohibition against doing it, deliberately made a number of agreed charges in a particular area for the purpose of eliminating other forms of transportation. In the first place, I think that that is an assumption that could scarcely be raised in practice because I think the kind of traffic that would have to be covered by the agreed charges to which I have just referred would cover so many items that in the first place it is unthinkable, even if the railroads were so intentioned, that they could arrive at that point. Second, I cannot help thinking that, even if a large part of the railway's traffic were affected by agreed charges, that would merely have the effect of opening new avenues of competition for the trucking industry. Therefore I do not believe that the railways are going to make a large number of agreed charges for the purpose of extinguishing or wiping out other forms of transportation.
But assuming for the moment that such a thing came about, and I cannot believe that it would, the fact remains that under subsection 2 of section 33 it would be considered a matter of public interest and the governor in council would have the right to refer the single agreed charge or the series of agreed charges to the board of transport commissioners which would have the fullest powers, as is perfectly obvious from reading the amendment.
Having regard to the fact that it is really only a theoretical necessity that the agreed charge should require to be compensatory, I think for all practical purposes this is taken care of adequately by the amendments we have discussed. Having thought about the matter very fully since the sittings of the committee, I have come to the conclusion that I could not accept any further amendment which was intended to say more specifically that the agreed charge should be compensatory. I think the bill was gone into with great care in the standing committee and I think that the amendments which have been suggested are an improvement on the bill as originally introduced and I hope that with the amendment the bill will commend itself to the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are three points in connection with this bill which I should like to place before the committee. The right of a railroad to enter into an agreed charge is a very drastic and far-reaching right which runs counter to our whole scheme of freight rates in Canada.

It is designed primarily for the purpose of meeting competition. It comes about in this way. A railroad can enter into an agreement, say with an automobile manufacturer, to carry 50 per cent, 75 per cent or 100 per cent of his product between two areas. With the traffic being tied up under an agreement of that kind, all other competitors are deprived of any chance of getting any of that business. So this right of making an agreed charge is a very powerful and drastic right. As I said a moment ago, it is designed for the one purpose of helping the railways to meet competition. The main provision of the act is contained in section 32, subsection 1, and when the amendment recommended by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines has been incorporated into that subsection it will read:
Notwithstanding anything in the Railway Act or in this act, a carrier may make such charges lor the transport from one point in Canada to another point in Canada of goods of a shipper as are agreed between the carrier and the shipper.
Before the committee a representative of the province of Manitoba urged that there be included in that subsection the words "to meet competition", so that the pertinent part of the subsection would then read:
Notwithstanding anything in the Railway Act or in this act, a carrier may to meet competition make such charges-
The minister was unwilling to accept that amendment in committee and I am going to suggest to him this afternoon that he give further consideration to the proposal by the government of Manitoba. I hope he will accept that amendment today. This idea of meeting competition is one reason why the railways are given the right to make an agreed charge and they should be restricted to the making of an agreed charge for the purpose of meeting competition. For example, without those words it would be possible for a railway to make an agreed charge with some company which happens to be a friend of the president of the railway company.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: They would have to be friends of both railway companies.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
That may be, but it might be possible for some firm to have friends in Montreal who are on the directorate of the Canadian Pacific Railway and thus be able to get an agreed charge. Surely there can be no objection to meeting the request of the government of Manitoba to add the words, "to meet competition" so that an agreed charge could be negotiated only for the purpose of meeting competition. That is my first point. It would do no harm to the bill to add those words and it would make it

clear in this key subsection of the bill that an agreed charge was for the purpose of meeting competition.
Then the minister dealt at some length this afternoon with another suggestion which was made in the standing committee, namely that there should be a provision written into this act that an agreed charge must be one that will at least pay the railway for carrying the goods; in other words, that they are not allowed to make an agreed charge which means carrying the goods at a loss. That is a very important matter for those of us who live on the west coast, because it is not so many years ago that the railways put out of business a steamship company operating between the west and east coasts and carrying goods at a lower rate than the railways had been carrying them. The railways put that steamship company out of business by dropping their rates below the rates the steamship company was charging. Then, once the steamship company had been put out of business the railways restored the rates to the old level.
I think it was clear that that was not done by way of an agreed charge, but rather by dropping the competitive rates. However, it could be done by agreed charges. We now have another line operating ships between Montreal and Vancouver and possibly through the St. Lawrence, though I am not sure about that. Of course they can carry goods cheaper by water through the Panama canal than the railways carry them overland.
On the west coast we cannot see any reason why our merchants and our consumers should not have the benefit of these cheap rates. There is the possibility here that the railways, by entering into agreed charges covering the bulk of the goods that are carried by ships, will be able to put that shipping line out of business.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: That would be because the rates were too low, would it not?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I would not quarrel with that, if the railways do not drop below what it costs them to carry the goods. But the minister has refused to write anything into this act which says the railways must not make an agreed charge which is below the cost of carrying the goods. That is where I quarrelled with him in the committee. He has refused to write in an amendment of that kind. I pointed out, and others in the committee supported me, that under the present agreed charge law, which is found in subsection 15 of the present section 32, the board of transport commissioners cannot allow an agreed charge to go into effect unless the railways show that the agreed charge will earn
Transport Act
them some money. In other words it should not mean that they would carry goods at a loss.
The minister meets my argument by saying, "You are trying to make the railways go back to the board of transport commissioners before an agreed charge can be put into effect".
I am doing no such thing. I am saying a provision should be written into section 32 that an agreed charge must be compensatory; in other words, no agreed charge can be below the actual cost to the railway. There are other similar provisions in section 32. Subclause 6 of this bill says:
An agreed charge shall be made on the established basis of rate making and shall be expressed in cents per hundred pounds or such other unit of weight or measurement as is appropriate; and the car-load rate for one car shall not exceed the carload rate for any greater number of cars.
The railways do not have to go to the board of transport commissioners about that, and nobody is asking that they should. I say, why could the minister not write in a clause 6 (a) which would say that the agreed charge shall be on a compensatory basis, in other words that it shall not be a charge which means carrying the goods at a loss? Then you would have that standard set up by the law that the railways must follow. I do not ask that the railways should have to go to the board of transport commissioners for prior approval, but I think the minister is carrying credulity a long way-

speechtext: Did you say "nobility?"

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: Credulity, perhaps that is the wrong word-when he takes the position, "the railways are not going to carry this business at a loss anyway; we shall leave it to them". The railways would carry goods at a loss fast, if they thought they would put that shipping line out of business that was carrying some of their traffic.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: They are doing it now in some places.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I think the minister is wrong in refusing to put in an amendment of this type. It is supposed to be another of the foundations for an agreed charge. This agreed charge law has been on the statute books since 1938, always on the basis that the rates must be compensatory, that there must be no cutting of costs by means of an agreed charge to such a great extent that the railway carries the goods at a loss. So I am hoping the minister will not be obdurate about this suggestion and will give further consideration to writing a provision into section 32 of the Transport Act that the rates must be compensatory.
The final point has to do with motor truck competition. The motor trucking industry is

Transport Act
very much afraid of this legislation because it believes this legislation is designed to enable the railways to drive them out of business. The C.P.R. representative made it very clear in the committee that the railways wanted an easing of the agreed charge provisions so they could put an end to rate cutting. He used words to this effect- unfortunately the transcript is not yet available-

speechtext: I shall let the hon. member have my copy if he would like it.

He said in effect the agreed charge puts an end to the rate cutting war. The truckers across this country-and there are many thousands of them carrying on well-established and well-conducted businesses- are afraid this law is designed to help the railways drive the truckers out of business. The only protection the minister is giving the trucking industry is what can be found in this new subclause 2 of section 33, which provides as follows: The governor in council- which, as you know, means the cabinet-if he has reason to believe that an agreed charge may be undesirable in the public interest, may refer the agreed charge to the board for investigation.
You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that this does not mention the trucking industry at all. It merely says the government can, if it believes that an agreed charge is undesirable in the public interest, refer that particular agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners. That may or may not meet the situation, but it is cold comfort. The trucking industry will have to go to the cabinet and sell the cabinet on the idea that a particular agreed charge is undesirable in the public interest.
We have had very convincing evidence in the last few weeks that some, at least, of the members of the cabinet take a whole lot of convincing. I am very doubtful whether this clause 2 of section 33 is worth the paper on which it is written. I hope it will be some protection, but I am very doubtful now whether anybody, the truckers, shipping people or anybody else, will ever be able to get very far under the terms of that clause.
There is a further right contained in the new section 33, subsection 1. The truckers asked that they be given the benefit of that subsection 1, which reads as follows:
Where an agreed charge has been in effect for at least three months
(a) any carrier, or association of carriers, by water or rail-
I point out that this cannot be attacked for a period of three months, and it only

covers a carrier under the Transport Act. It is not of any benefit whatever to the trucking industry. As a matter of fact it is of no benefit to a shipping firm doing business beyond the island of Orleans, because the Transport Act only applies to the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river as far as the island of Orleans; also on the Mackenzie river system. It does not apply on the west coast, and it does not apply in the maritime provinces. Therefore the words, "any carrier, or association of carriers, by water or rail" are very restrictive. Then the section continues:
(b) any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality-
The right of any one individual shipper to complain is taken away. It can now only be an association of shippers. You will notice there is no mention of the trucking industry there at all. The section continues:
-may complain to the minister that the agreed charge is unjustly discriminatory against it or places its business at an unfair disadvantage, and the minister may, if he is satisfied-
That section will now read:
-the minister may, if he is satisfied that in the public interest the complaint should be investigated, refer the complaint to the board for investigation.
That subsection provides that any carrier under the act, or an association of shippers, can complain not to the cabinet but to the minister and then if he thinks there is discrimination the minister can refer the agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners. I believe the minister might very well have given that protection to an association of motor vehicle transport operators. I made a motion accordingly in the committee, and I believe they should have been given the right to apply to the minister in the hope that he would then refer the complaint to the board of transport commissioners.
It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that the government is not facing up to the facts of life in regard to transport in Canada. The government has no national transport policy. Some years ago the royal commission on transportation headed by Hon. Mr. Turgeon dealt with the question of a national transport policy. Very little has been done to work out such a policy, and in fact we have none today. The railways and some shipping are under the dominion; the trucks are under the provinces; pipe lines, which are another means of transport, are in part under the dominion, and there is great confusion in the transport industry in Canada.
I do not believe the minister can simply push the motor truck industry into the

background and not have them given some consideration under federal legislation. In some of the provinces, notably Manitoba and British Columbia, the railways, although they come under dominion jurisdiction, are able to go to the provincial transport boards and complain about the rates being charged by the trucks.

speechtext: In British Columbia and Manitoba I believe that is right. There was also evidence given the other day that in the minister's province of Quebec they can do that.

They have the right to appear before the provincial body in Quebec, and in Ontario they have the right to appear and protest the granting of a licence for a route to a trucker. It seems to me that in view of the fact that we have no over-all transportation policy, the trucking industry has a right to ask that it be allowed at least to make representations to the minister under this new section 33 in respect to agreed charges. There should be reciprocity. If the provinces are going to hear the railways, then I think the dominion should make some provision at least for the trucking people to be heard when the question of agreed charges is involved to the extent that it may be running them out of business.
Those are the three points I wish to place before the minister this afternoon. I hope he will give consideration to further amendments to the bill. There is no reason why this situation I have mentioned could not be remedied today. I think if steps of that kind are taken, then this bill as it goes back to the house will be a great improvement on the bill in its present form.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I should like to deal with just one phase arising out of the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra having to do with motor truckers in the various provinces of this country. I hold no brief, indirectly or at all, for them, but I believe in a measure of equality of opportunity and in fairness to all. I cannot understand why under the new section 33 motor truckers should be denied the equality of opportunity and equality of complaint that other recognized carriers under the law have.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra suggested to the minister that some amendment at this time might be acceptable. I think today we witnessed something in the history of parliament, when parliament was not only supreme but sublime in the stand taken by the Prime Minister. I suggest that
Transport Act
a similar attitude in respect to this matter on the part of the minister would further the recognition of the fact that parliament is made up of a government and an opposition, and that the opposition's function is not "to oppose everything and propose nothing", to use the Tierney epigram, but is to advance arguments and through a community of counsel arrive at what is best in the drafting of legislation. Certainly parliament had an example of that today. Parliament showed itself sublime in the maintenance of parliamentary supremacy and supreme in the carrying out of that function and responsibility.
I ask the minister why the motor transport industry of this country should not have an equal opportunity to complain. That would not mean they were going to secure any advantages over railway transport. It simply asks, it simply suggests, it simply demands that they have the right to complain. Why should the minister not accept the suggestion that when any agreed charge has been in effect for at least three months any carrier, by water or rail or motor transport, or any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality may complain to the minister that the agreed charge is unjustly discriminatory against a carrier or shipper, or places his business at an unfair disadvantage? Then the minister, if he is satisfied that in the public interest the complaint should be investigated, may refer the complaint to the board for investigation.
The motor transport industry, the truckers across Canada, have a large investment. In no way do I plead that they should be placed in an advantageous position, but why should they be placed in a position where the railway companies or any other carriers have the privilege of fixing their rates at an uneconomical and unprofitable level, and thereby through unfair competition destroy a competitive carrier? Certainly the experience in other fields of endeavour so far as monopoly privilege is concerned is that when it is uncontrolled and not subject to punishment by the state it brings about the destruction of its competitors through the use of its financial resources and the power of its authority to interfere with competition among those less favourably placed.
The reason we have the Combines Investigation Act is to protect the public interest against injustices that might be perpetrated against weaker competitors. No one in business has the right to expect a market to be provided for him, but the essence of free enterprise is that each, whether great and powerful or weak, shall have equal opportunity in the market that is available. Why should the motor transport groups across the

Transport Act
country, the various truckers, be placed in the position where, no matter how unjust, unfair and discriminatory a rate may be, they cannot even have the privilege of making a complaint to the minister? If they do make a complaint it will be in the nature of a gratuitous complaint upon which the minister cannot act, no matter whether he concludes that what has taken place is unjust and undesirable in the public interest.
What possible justification can there be for placing those who have invested their money in private industry and who are in a legitimate line of business in the position of not being permitted to complain that unfairness is being perpetrated against them and unjust agreed charges are being promulgated and utilized? I ask the minister to reconsider his stand, for certainly unless section 33 as it now stands is amended it simply means that any railway company or other carrier in this country can put into effect agreed charges that will be so low and uneconomical as to secure all the business available, which will place them in the position, having secured the business and driven out competitors, of being able to raise their charges again when the competition is removed.
The section in its present form is an invitation to destroy the competition of the motor transport industry. Under the law as it is now being brought into effect the motor transport industry has no right to be unjust and unfair to the railway companies, and there is every power to prevent them being so. Should they not also be placed in the position where gross unfairness to them will mean that they will at least be permitted to make a complaint so the minister, having considered their complaint and concluded that the rate is discriminatory or the agreed charge is undesirable in the public interest, will be free to refer the question to the board in order that the whole matter may be investigated and a fair and proper decision arrived at?
I must say that the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is a challenging one. On the face of the argument advanced and on the knowledge I have of the difficulties in connection with that type of competition, I must say that his suggestion would assure at least a modicum of fairness to an industry that has been built up and has expanded tremendously in recent years. So there will be no misunderstanding, I repeat that I want to see no unfairness on the part of the motor transport industry as against other carriers, but I do not want to be a party in parliament to placing the other carriers in a position where they are above 
those rules of fairness and justice, those considerations of the public interest, which certainly should be the concern of parliament but which will not be provided unless a change is made in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group pretty well take the same attitude toward the bill as previous speakers. Sitting in this corner of the house we very often find ourselves at a slight disadvantage, in that the arguments are sometimes fairly well covered by the time our turn to speak arrives. But I do wish to say a word or two along the same line, and to go on record as supporting the trucking industry at least to the extent that they should have the right to complain to the minister, and that right should be written into the legislation.
This is something the members of this group who were on the committee suggested at the time. In fact I proposed an amendment in the committee and asked for a recorded vote. The amendment was defeated. The minister did not feel he could lend his support to my amendment, and as a result it was lost.
It is all very well to say that the trucking industry can complain if it wishes. That is not a very weighty argument, because I know I could make complaints if I wanted to, or John Doe on the street could make complaints. We could all do that, and write to the minister; but unless what we want is written into the legislation it will do very little good to those who are vitally interested in the matter of transportation.
We heard from counsel representing the railway companies and, like good lawyers, they made a good case. I fancy if the same lawyers had been employed to argue on the other side they could have made just as good a case. So I do not place very much stock in the arguments of corporation lawyers.
There are other people who have studied this problem and who do not speak on behalf of any particular corporation. They speak for those interests for which they feel they are responsible. When the board of transport commissioners met some months ago some distinguished witnesses appeared before it and gave evidence as to why the agreed charge, as it was understood at that time, should not be permitted to remain. When the board met in Edmonton I noted that both the mayor of Calgary and the mayor of Edmonton appeared and presented arguments which, in my view, were very strong indeed. When Mayor MacKay of Calgary appeared before the board he said that the principle of agreed charges should find itself completely and without reservation included in the one and one-third rule. He added that the

railways' new wrinkle, as he described it, was a woeful disregard of the intent of that principle. That is pretty strong language, and it does not come from just any Joe on the street; it comes from the mayor of an important city. The press article quotes the mayor further in these words:
We cannot continue to favour one section of the country at the expense of the other, and excuse ourselves on the theory that western provinces must be sacrificed upon the altar of competition that may exist on the coastal waterfronts of this country.
The mayor of Edmonton made statements along similar lines. Mayor Hawrelak of that city said that agreed charges were a calculated and deliberate attempt on the part of the railways to circumvent short-haul rates to Alberta that were exacted three years ago. The newspaper article quotes him further as stating:
We suggest that the present result of the application of agreed charges has been mischievous and has resulted in absurd consequences.
To say the least that is strong language, but it comes from men who should know what they are talking about. Then Mr. McCullough appeared on behalf of the federation of automobile dealers' associations and, according to the article in the press, said:
If the agreed charge method of freight rates is applied to the movement of automobiles, the highway transport of automobiles and trucks from eastern to western Canada will disappear altogether.
While the minister and those who are responsible for the present bill may not express alarm and may not feel too greatly concerned that the trucking industry will suffer, the fact of the matter is that some of the long-distance automobile conveyors are going off the road right now. I am told they are standing idle in some of the used car lots because there is no further use for them.
My information is that large sums of money have been invested by the trucking industry in the construction of refrigerated trucks, and that this policy of agreed charges will result in a tremendous loss in that connection. In the trucking industry refrigerated vehicles are an innovation, but considerable sums of money have been invested in this kind of equipment.
The concession asked by the trucking industry was not unreasonable. Their amendment was very simple, and I cannot see why the minister could not have agreed to it. The amendment states that-
Any carrier, or association of carriers, by water or rail-

And then they advocate the addition of these words:
-or any motor vehicle transport operator, or association of motor vehicle transport operators,
or-
They asked only to be included with others in the right to appeal to the minister. They said, "Give us the same right as anybody else." For the life of me I cannot see why an amendment of that kind could not have been accepted.
In committee I asked one of the witnesses if he would agree that the principle of agreed charges was similar to that of the loss leader in merchandising. The minister interjected by stating, "It cannot be like the loss leader principle, because an agreed charge must be compensatory." I did not go into any detailed argument, but I must admit I am somewhat confused as to the exact meaning of "compensatory" when used in this connection.
I do not claim to be an expert in matters of cost accounting but, in a small way, I do know that if a person is going to make a profit on an article or a service, then of necessity he must bring into his accounting every possible cost that could be included in the manufacture of that article. He would have to include depreciation on his building; he would have to include amortization of loans. So far as I can see, in respect of compensatory charges the bill is worded in such a way that I doubt very much whether all the cost factors in an agreed charge are included. For instance, I do not know whether depreciation of trackage would be calculated in that computation. If all that is calculated in the costs involved in an agreed charge is what it costs to run a train, then I cannot see how that could be considered a compensatory rate. Possibly they would have to figure out everything it takes to run the railroad across that particular given mileage.
If it does not take into account all the cost factors, then I claim it would be something akin to the principle of the loss leader. If that is to be done, then I would say the only reason it would be done would be to cut the throat of the trucking industry. I hope it will not be done. If it is done, there is no recourse. It is not written into the legislation that the trucking industry, which is a very considerable industry now, has the right to go through the proper channels and make their complaints.
I shall not take up any more time of the committee, Mr. Chairman. I know the minister and the government are aware that as time passes by industries arise which for a few years are inconsequential, but eventually they become part of our national life. Take the

Transport Act
trucking industry. A few years ago a five-ton truck was considered to be a pretty hefty truck. It was not much of a threat to the railroad. The same can be said of airplanes. But as time went by a five-ton truck became a very small truck. Farmers used them. For instance there was a time when cattle were driven into the stockyard in the small town and then shipped by rail. In most of these small towns now, as you pass by them, you see these stockades. They may just as well not be there; they are seldom used. Why? Because today the farmer puts his stock, his hogs, or whatever he has, in his five or ten-ton truck and hauls them 100 miles, to the nearest city where there is a packing plant. That has happened because the process of time has brought certain types of progress to us. Today it is not a five-ton truck or even a ten-ton truck. It is not unusual to find on our highways today a 25,000-ton truck.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a minute or two to place before the minister specific examples of the things about which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Prince Albert, and my colleague, the hon. member for Macleod, were speaking. I want to bring this to the attention of the minister because it does exemplify the thing about which the hon. members have been complaining, and I think it will convey to the minister the need for doing something that affects not only the trucking industry-I am not complaining about that-but the people themselves
Here is the situation. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the Hart highway was completed about two years ago between Prince George and Dawson Creek. Trucks began hauling great quantities of goods over the Hart highway from Prince George into the Peace river bloc of British Columbia, serving that whole area that had not been served by a railway except the Northern Alberta

railway as it comes in from Edmonton as far as Dawson Creek in British Columbia.
Almost immediately the truck traffic began to grow in size the railways, the Canadian National Railways in particular, entered into agreements with shippers up in the Peace river bloc to bring 50,000-pound carload lots of certain kinds of goods into Dawson Creek at a rate of $1.50 per hundredweight from Vancouver. The only way they could get to Dawson Creek, British Columbia, from Vancouver would be around by way of Edmonton, then up over the Northern Alberta railway line through Grande Prairie and into Dawson Creek, which would be, I would say conservatively, 800 to 850 miles farther than it would be directly from Vancouver to Prince George and then by truck across the Hart highway and into Dawson Creek. The regular rate from Vancouver by way of the Canadian National Railways and the Northern Alberta railway, just to Grande Prairie, which is 90 miles less in distance, is $2.44. In fact it has been $2.44 for quite a long time. The situation is simply this. The railways, in order to destroy-not just to meet-the competition, to destroy the truck competition up into the Peace river bloc of British Columbia, introduced this new rate. It has been found by competent investigators that the rate is below the cost of haul. It is not compensatory. A good many protests were made on the ground that the rate is not compensatory. I agree with my hon. friends when they say that whenever the railways do set up a rate under the agreed charge provision of the act, which is a reduced rate to meet competition, they should go to the board of transport commissioners to make absolutely certain that it is compensatory. It should be written into the act. May I draw to the attention of the minister-

It may interest the minister to know that boards of trade and chambers of commerce all over that north country have had their statisticians and accountants working on this ever since last fall, and the conclusions they have come to are that they must be non-compensatory rates. They tried to figure it out, but they have not access to all the figures and, as the hon. member for Macleod said, it is difficult for a layman to know what does constitute the true cost of hauling by rail. I am told they have several devices they can use on occasion to indicate that they are not charging the full cost of hauling. They can draw something out of the hat to support whatever contention they may be making. I agree at once with the minister that no one will know whether these rates are compensatory until such time as the board of transport commissioners examines them. I believe there is considerable evidence available to show that they believe they are.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister to show how ridiculous these things can become, when an agreed charge of this kind is applied in one area and other areas nearby examine the situation. This happened in the Peace river bloc in Alberta. They found that they could ship goods by carload into Dawson Creek, which is 90 miles further along than Grande Prairie, haul them back that 90 miles by truck and still save 59 cents per hundredweight on the carload.
That is the sort of thing that drives people wild; that is the sort of thing that makes it necessary for shippers to resort to many things which should not be necessary. For instance, instead of shipping their goods directly to Grande Prairie where they need them, they find they can save money by shipping from Vancouver to Dawson Creek and then hiring trucks to haul them back. By that method they deny the railroad the rates which they normally would charge, rates that would be fair, rates the railroads could get. They are denying the railroads business and the railroads do not seem to realize that they are cutting their own throats by this price cutting, this business of trying to get below the actual cost of transportation.
When a ridiculous situation like that develops the railroads discover that they have
Transport Act
lost something on their year's business and they come to parliament to ask for a grant. I submit that wherever the railroads have lost business they should show that they have not been cutting rates below cost; otherwise we should not be subsidizing them in order to help them destroy their competitors.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we all realize that the two large railroads and the smaller ones are having a most difficult time getting along and showing a profit, or even keeping in business. I believe the railroads have had the most difficult time of any business in Canada over the last 40 years. The Canadian National Railways have continued to lose money for the taxpayers of Canada, and have had to be subsidized by the country. But when we find that the boards of strategy of the railroads figure they can make money by cutting rates so low that they can put the trucking concerns out of business I think we should stop such nonsense and face [DOT]this transportation situation fairly and squarely.
If this country had a population of 30 million people we would be able to use our waterways for the transport of goods to a much greater extent. In other parts of the world, such as the countries bordering on the Danube, the Thames, the Rhine and many other great waterways, they are manufacturing goods which compete against the manufactured products of this country. Those countries use the cheapest forms of transportation; they utilize their canals, rivers and inland lakes. Unfortunately the population of Canada is not large enough to permit the use of small trading ships from port to port on the great lakes. Such pick-up ships could be used, and then they could transship to larger ships coming in from Europe or going out from this country.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned one ambitious shipping company which endeavoured to give the people of Canada a cheap and efficient transportation service. However, the railroads who come to parliament for subsidies brought the rates down so low that this shipping company was put out of business. That case should be investigated. I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra believes that the facts he outlined were the truth, and if that is so no contribution should be made to the railroads by the taxpayers of Canada.
I can remember when a ship owned by the Kirkwood Steamship Company plied between Hamilton, Toronto and Vancouver. A great deal of enthusiasm developed over this service, but it lasted for only a season or two. The idea was to ship manufactured products and other commodities from the east to the

Transport Act
west and then transship for the prairie provinces. They could undercut the railroads.
The people of Canada are looking for methods that will advance progress in this country, and we should do everything in our power to turn out goods and services at the least possible cost. The railroads would be better off, and so would the brains of the railroads who now work out the sort of thing referred to by the previous speaker, where goods are shipped 900 miles at a cost of $1.50 per hundredweight, then sent back by truck 90 miles at a cost of 50 cents, making a total cost of $2 as compared with the direct freight rate of $2.40. Anyone who knows anything about transportation knows that is a crazy and ridiculous situation. There is something wrong.
I hold no brief for the truckers or for the railroad companies; the only brief I hold is for fair play and proper treatment for the citizens of Canada. We wonder why the railroads are losing money, but I can give a case from my own experience. A freight agent came to me and wanted to know why I was not shipping by Canadian National. I was bringing in thousands of tons of freight a year. I asked him if he was sure they could do the job. I had seven pieces of valuable, necessary and short-supply machinery shipped from Chicago by rail. When they arrived in Collingwood five of the seven pieces were lying on their sides, damaged to such an extent that it took six months to get them back into working condition. I did not want compensation in the form of money; I wanted the machines, which were urgent and necessary.
The railroad adjuster came to see me but I was not interested in how it happened. He said, "That is the shunting engine; they have shunted it and knocked it around." He said they would pay for it, but who wants to be paid when you have to wait six months before you can use your machines? I can assure you that I have never shipped a dollar's worth of goods by railroad since that time. If they do not give service to the public of Canada and cannot stay in business without having the protection of this government, the sooner they are both out of business the better. I believe there is a great need for the railroads, but I believe there is a great need for far more headwork on behalf of the railroads in many ways that will ensure their success and stop their nonsense of cutting rates in order to put a man or a concern out of business.
The first railroad in Canada ran from the city of Toronto to the town of Newmarket in 1845. In the second year they ran to my home town of Collingwood, and the following

year they ran the railroad from Toronto to Montreal. At that time the trains travelled at about 14 miles an hour. Today the roadbed is so lousy-and there is no other word for it, because it causes you extra travel-that the average rate of speed allowed to the engineers is 35 miles an hour. Who in the world would want to take three hours to travel 90 miles, when they can travel it by car in two hours on a four-lane highway?
I have a pass on the railroad, but I do not use it because I would have to sit in the city of Toronto for one hour longer than I want to, which I am forced to do if I use the railroad. I must sit in the oldest, most dilapidated cars on the C.N.R. railroad for three hours. I would far prefer to use my own motor car and have my wife drive me to Toronto and back than use the pass to travel on that railroad.
There is room for improvement. People did not wish to travel for such a long time on the railroad from Meaford to Toronto on a Sunday night on almost the oldest railroad line in Canada. The result was that that line had to be taken out of service this year. Some people were horrified because they were going to cut out this service, but if the railroad line does not pay and is calling on the taxpayers of Canada to make it pay, it should be stopped. That railroad could have been made to pay if they had travelled the 90 miles in 1J hours. Then you would not see many people using motor cars.
I lived in Philadelphia for some years. It is 90 miles from Philadelphia to New York. Every hour on the hour a train leaves Philadelphia and a train leaves New York, and they travel that distance in one hour and fifteen minutes day in and day out. Let us get down to having a real country with real railroads. Let us face up to the facts and cut out the lines that are not paying, and not try to put a firm out of business by giving ridiculously low rates. Let everybody-the truckers, the steamship companies and the airline companies-appeal to the Minister of Transport for fairness and justice. Do not leave this in the hands of people who say that the only method of survival is to put a trucking firm or a trucker out of business. These people are entitled to justice the same as any other body of people. They all look to parliament for such justice. I am sure the minister wishes to give justice to the most lowly and humble as well as the highest.

Mi. Hamilton (York West): As a matter of fact, if I have got off to a bad start it is because I am unaccustomed to my lofty surroundings in this row in the house. It seems to me that the major problem we are facing here is that we are making a deviation from the normal line of rate making for railway transportation companies. I am wondering if it cannot be traced back to the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, when he indicated that we appeared to lack a firm national policy in connection with transportation matters.
It might be wise for the minister to consider an investigation of some kind into all the problems of the railways in connection with their rate making position, and also the various problems which confront the shippers, as referred to by the hon. member for Simcoe North, the truckers, and the latest addition to the large bulk carriers, the airlines. I am sure there are a few problems that are going to require some fairly close attention in the near future.
It appears that in connection with this problem of agreed charges we are swinging over from the position formerly taken and expressed, I think, in the Railway Act, that the railways are common carriers and to a great extent public utilities, and that in their position, dealing with specific problems of rate making, those problems are of national interest. When we come down to the problem of agreed charges it seems that we are substituting the yardstick of public interest for national interest, and it may be that we must look at the plight of other transportation companies, the truckers, the airlines, the shippers, in a wider sense than that which is envisaged under the agreed rate charge set-up.
I point this out because I believe the railways have existed to a great extent because of the role they have played in the national interest. Now we are allowing them to move their arguments into the realm of public interest in a manner which may very definitely affect the fortunes of the other types of carriers. I am sure no one can point his finger at me and say this is a strong argument against the railway position. I happen to be the son of a railway man, and I have heard the arguments of the railways put forth on a broad and sound basis for many years. But when we start to deal with the public interest in any given locality, it may be that they are allowing a system to creep in which may affect the other methods of transportation on a national basis, and it is going to be a problem of ours to see that there is no legislation or there should be no legislation which will have that overriding effect.
Transport Act
One of the things I have seen here is the chance that with this type of agreed charge rate making we may in fact be legislating against decentralizing of industry. I believe everybody in this house has said from time to time that one of the most important things we must look for in the future of Canada is the spreading out of industry from one end of the country to the other. Let me take this as a specific example. Someone establishes a new plant in the west. He establishes it at a certain place because the labour market is good. He is close to a concentrated public demand for his product. He is in a position then to set up business, and he may have a very good price, competitive with a firm which is manufacturing in one of the populated areas in eastern Canada, Montreal, Toronto or some place like that.
Now, the manufacturer in eastern Canada goes to the railway and enters into an agreement for an agreed charge to the western area. The new manufacturer out there has invested his capital and may be the sole or major industry in the town; the employees are dependent upon him for their livelihood. The agreed charge given to the processor in eastern Canada enables him to lay down the product in that western market at a price less than that at which it can be produced right at the place where the public demand for it exists.
That manufacturer in the west may say, "I am going to complain about this." As I understand the provisions, he complains and what is his answer? He is told, ''We will give you the same treatment as is given to the other manufacturer. You may now ship your product to Toronto or Montreal at the same rate the manufacturer there can ship his product out west." Obviously that is no answer to his problem. He has located there because he is in a position to meet competition, which is on a high level of production, and to supply his market at a reasonable price. He is not in a position to enter into an agreed charge, probably because of higher overhead, higher wages and perhaps the market is not as large. He is not in a position to ship back into the concentrated area and take advantage of an agreed charge. I would say this was one of the failures of the so-called complaint system which is provided by this legislation. I would suggest to the minister it certainly would bear looking into.
If we are switching over, if we are entering into a new phase of rate making, then I feel we should insist upon ironclad rules in connection with the compensatory provisions. We have been asking the question, what does compensatory mean? Boiling it down to layman's language, it probably means any rate

Transport Act
has to give back to the carrier all his costs plus something to boot. If this particular formula is not adhered to, then I think it will result in what I started out to prove following the line of public interest; we are going to be in a position where the national interest will not be served in that the competing services will not be able to bear up under that type of competition.
I believe one of the speakers here used the term "loss leader''. I feel it would be easy enough in various places in the country, where there is a concentration of population and of manufacturing resources, to force other modes of competition out of the picture by the use of this method of rate making. If they are forced out of the picture there, we cannot expect them to carry on in what we term the fringe areas.
There is one other thing I have noticed about this particular legislation. It seems to me that here again we are faced with what we are faced with in connection with many pieces of legislation that come before us. We are substituting the discretion of the minister for the opinion of a board. Where previously matters of this kind came before a board, we now concentrate the power in the hands of a minister and say, "You make up your mind as to whether or not there is a valid complaint in this case."
These amendments do not go the whole way. I do not think anyone took the position that was taken by the truckers' association. I believe it is agreed that we should not put anything in the administrative way of the railways being able to make quick decisions, being able to more or less make decisions on the spot in connection with this type of rate making. I do not believe the amendment .suggested in committee by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra did go the whole way. It did not say that as soon as an agreed charge was published the truckers should be allowed to bring a complaint.
As I recall the hon. member's amendment, it allowed the agreement in respect of the agreed charge to be entered into by the shipper and the railway, and if after the three months had elapsed a complaint arose, that was the time for the truckers' association to be included in the group of people who could bring their complaint forward and have it heard.
Certainly this does not seem to be asking too much. It is difficult to understand what does amount to discrimination here. I feel people should be allowed to come into some of these hearings in the same way I know they can before the air transport board, as a member of the general public. If such a person wished to put some representations

in writing he is given an opportunity to be heard. Here are a group of people who are as close to this situation as they possibly could be, and they are not given an opportunity to be heard.
It seems to me this has nothing whatever to do with the efficacy of the legislation; whether they have a good complaint or a bad complaint has nothing to do with the right to be heard. Surely the minister might think again about what we all feel is a very reasonable request. We are not taking sides in the matter, but these people should be allowed to come forward if they think they have been hurt and put their case in a reasonable manner.

speechtext: Is the minister going to deal with these points that have been raised?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
Yes, I am, Mr. Chairman. Quite a number of points have been raised during the discussion this afternoon, and I shall try to deal with them in the order in which they were raised during the discussion.
The first is a suggestion that we should include, in subsection 1 I think it was, the words "in order to meet competition". A good deal of stress has been laid on the fact that agreed charges are an instrument intended to meet competition. As I said in the standing committee, I do not think we could properly put those words in the definition of an agreed charge without creating difficulties which I think ought to be avoided.
When the subject was discussed in the standing committee I referred to an agreed charge that had been made for the carriage of canned goods between points in eastern Canada and points in western Canada which, in fact, were points situate either in British Columbia or Alberta. This agreed charge, which I think is typical of quite a number of agreed charges that have been made by the railways and shippers, provides altogether for, I suppose, 50 different points of destination. If we insert the words, "in order to meet competition", that is going to have the effect of excluding from the benefit of an agreed charge any point at which there is not in fact competition with rail services.
During the discussion before the committee I tried to pick out one of the points in British Columbia which might not have truck competition with the rails. Unfortunately I picked the wrong place, and I was told it was right in the middle of Vancouver. But I think it is quite possible to find that among the destinations included in almost any agreed charge there are several that are not served by other means of transport. Therefore if you include the words that the agreed charge

must be "in order to meet competition", you thereby exclude consignees in those places from having the benefits of an agreed charge. Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I had to say in the committee that I was not prepared to accept that amendment.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra laid a certain amount of stress on the fact that this amendment had been suggested by the representative of the province of Manitoba, and therefore I should perhaps reconsider the question. But, Mr. Chairman, after the committee had met on the subject I received, quite unsolicited, a note from Mr. Shepard, who was the representative of the province of Manitoba, in which he said to me:
Manitoba's suggested amendment to section 32, subsection 1, is no longer necessary in the light of your proposed amendment to section 33.
I think that should dispose effectively of the suggestion that we would improve the agreed charge, as something which is of benefit to shippers and consignees, by restricting it in this way. I think there is no doubt that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra would like to improve it. He would like to see the agreed charge as an instrument of competition, as we all regard it. I consider there is a great difference between describing it as an instrument of competition and using words which in effect preclude non-competitive points from having any advantage from it. Therefore I hope the hon. member will not further urge such an amendment.
The next point that was raised was that the agreed charge ought to be compensatory. I should like to tell hon. members what has been the experience under the existing legislation. Before doing so, I should like to emphasize the fact that the agreed charge has formed part of the Transport Act since it was introduced in 1938. It is not a new device at all. It is not a new method of rate making, as seems to have been suggested this afternoon. It is merely a way by which carrier and shipper can get together and agree on terms for carriage of a part or all of the shipper's goods to be transported between one group of points of origin and, let us say, another group of points of destination. The practice has been in effect since 1938. What we are proposing to do now is not to institute another and different scheme of rate making but, if I may use very simple language, we are endeavouring to streamline the procedure for making an agreed charge effective.
I told the committee there have been cases under the present legislation in which an agreed charge has been arrived at between the carrier and the shipper and submitted to
Transport Act
the board at the end of April or early in May, and because someone represented to the board that he wished to make representations concerning the agreed charge approval was delayed until the month of September. Under the present legislation everybody who is interested in postponing the coming into effect of an agreed charge will naturally object so as to delay the' evil day, let us say, as long as possible.
What we are doing under this bill is to arrive at a simpler procedure, one by which the agreed charge takes effect from the time the contract is made between the parties and filed with the board, and after notice is given in accordance with the provisions of the bill that is now before us. In other words the agreed charge is not a new method of arriving at the charge to be made for the transport of goods. The agreed charge has long been established in England and has been part of our transport law in Canada since 1938.
There seems to be an impression that during the last period of approximately 17 years agreed charges have been used to carry goods at rates which were less than compensatory. Nothing could be further from the fact. In the first place, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out, the existing law requires the board of transport commissioners, in considering an agreed charge, to see what is the effect on the net revenue of the carrier. Therefore, so far as what has happened up to date is concerned, it cannot be said that an agreed charge has been made that was not compensatory, because that was one of the points which the board had to check before granting approval of the agreed charge under the present legislation.
In the committee it was suggested that an agreed charge had been used to put out of business the operations of a company called Monsen-Clarke which at some time a number of years ago, around 1949 I think it was-perhaps it was 1938 or 1939-
