I understood it was 1949, but the date really is not material. It was stated before the committee, and I think in perfect good faith, that the reason this shipping company had gone out of business was that agreed charges had been made which were non-compensatory. This was stated to be the reason this company had been put out of business. When I had the opportunity of inquiring into the facts I found that no transcontinental agreed charge had been made until several years after the company had

Transport Act
given up business, and therefore it was manifest that agreed charges had no influence whatsoever in respect of the decision of this company.
One fact which I think must be borne in mind in considering competition between rail and ship is the fact that where, as in the case referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, there was a shipping service established from the east cost of Canada to Vancouver, the rail companies were entitled under the Railway Act to put in competitive rates in order to enable them to compete with the shipping companies. Everyone who knows the Railway Act knows that under section 334 the companies may be required to establish that these rates are compensatory. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I do not really believe one can point a finger at agreed charges and say that instrument put out of business a shipping company which was providing a service to the west coast.
In considering such competition there is a rather important distinction to be made between agreed charges and competitive rates. As I understand the law, the railway companies may establish competitive rates as long as the competition is there, and the moment the competition ceases the rate ceases. But an agreed charge is an entirely different thing. An agreed charge is made for a term and continues to be operative until the end of that term or until, pursuant to the provision of the proposed legislation so far as the future is concerned, one party gives notice to the other after a whole year that he wishes to terminate the agreement. So there is a marked difference between competitive rates which are, let us say, temporary and ephemeral, and the agreed charges which must exist for a specified term.
I would also like to touch on the subject of whether there is adequate provision in the draft bill now before the committee to cover the question of whether or not an agreed charge must be compensatory. I think I made it perfectly clear that there is not in Bill 449 the same kind of clause as there is in the existing legislation. But I do not believe the matter can be solved in the simple fashion which was suggested earlier this afternoon, namely that all one has to do is say something along these lines, "An agreed charge shall be compensatory."

speechtext: Was that not the intention?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I think, if I might answer the question before going back to my argument, it is perfectly clear from the bill now before the committee that the agreed charge must be compensatory because, as I shall show in a moment, the question of whether it is or is not

compensatory is one of the first things ivith which the board must deal when the agreed charge is referred to it. I shall come back to that later. I am not running away from it, but I would prefer to develop the argument in the way in which it was offered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. He says, in effect, the law should say, "An agreed charge shall be compensatory". But unfortunately that is not a thing which can be determined in the same simple fashion as the other matters which are referred to in subsection 6. Subsection 6 covers two or three points. It says that-
An agreed charge shall be made on the established basis of rate making-
There cannot be any quarrel about whether it is or whether it is not on the established basis. No one has any interest in departing from the established basis. Then it says- -and shall be expressed in cents per hundred pounds or such other unit of weight or measurement as is appropriate-[DOT]
It seems to me that does not lend itself to much interpretation. And then it continues: -and the car-load rate for one car shall not exceed the car-load rate for any greater number of cars.
That, it seems to me, is also something that does not require any examination or consideration. When you say that an agreed charge shall be compensatory, while for the sake of satisfying my hon. friend I would like to put that in, I do not believe it would dispose of the matter, because that is an incomplete provision. One would have to go on and give power to the board of transport commissioners to determine it. That involves some reference at some stage to the board of transport commissioners for the express purpose of determining whether or not a rate is compensatory. And that I think, as I said earlier, is just another difficulty of procedure which would be added to something which is intended to be simple, and which is intended to provide an effective instrument of competition.
Leaving aside for the moment the desirability of having some simple phrase of that nature, such as is suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, surely it is impossible to examine the legislation and conclude that it is not clearly intended that an agreed charge shall be compensatory. We find in subsection 3 of the amendment:
In dealing with a reference under this section the board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant, including the effect that the making of the agreed charges has had or is likely to have on the net revenue of the carriers who are parties to it-*
That of course is not saying specifically that they shall be compensatory; but that is

the language which is used in the present law, and obviously when you say, "examine the effect on the net revenue" this is merely another way of saying that agreed charges shall be remunerative or compensatory.
Therefore I do not think there is any purpose in suggesting that, if the board at some stage or another may be called upon to look into the effect of an agreed charge on the net revenue of the carrier, any further provision is necessary to warn the carrier that the charge must be compensatory, because I infer that the board of transport commissioners on a reference would cancel it or vary it, just as they could refuse to approve it under existing legislation.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, after thinking about the practical effect of putting in some such provision as that I have just referred to, I came to the conclusion that there was no better way of dealing with this question of the compensatory aspect of an agreed charge than is done under this draft amendment, and that in fact was done under the original bill itself.
I would like to say one further word with regard to agreed charges. There does seem to be the impression prevailing, at least among some members, that the agreed charge is some kind of cut rate. I would like to go back to what was said a moment ago by the hon. member for Peace River-and I shall deal with that presently-but it does seem to me that there is an impression that an agreed charge is a cut rate.
Not only is there no evidence of the railways making agreed charges at rates less than cost, but the board of transport commissioners way-bill studies showed that agreed charges are among the most remunerative of railway rates. For instance, last year the average ton-mile revenue of railways from all their traffic approximated 1J cents, in contrast with 3J cents from agreed charge traffic. So that in round figures it was about 2 cents a ton-mile higher f>r agreed charges than it was for the general run of their other business.
I think that should dispose of the thought that agreed charges are some form of cut rate introduced to get business at a loss. There is no such thing as agreed charges at a loss at the moment because, as I said a moment ago, there is this express provision that the agreed charge must be compensatory; and I think this is adequately taken care of in the legislation we are now talking about.
I should like now to talk about the right of those engaged in the motor transport industry to complain against an agreed charge.
Transport Act
The first point I would emphasize is that, despite what has been said, the motor transport industry is not a regulated industry. We heard some very interesting evidence before the committee with respect to the extent of regulation, and I do not think it is an exaggeration of the situation when I say there is virtually no regulation of rates in the trucking industry at the present time, and certainly no regulation of interprovincial highway transport.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra referred to regulation in British Columbia. I do not know whether the railways are permitted to complain against rates fixed by whatever regulatory body there may be in British Columbia. I know in the province of Quebec, to which he refers, that the railways have been permitted to present evidence with regard to public convenience and necessity, when it came to the granting of a franchise to an operator. But my understanding is that there is no discussion on the question of rates, and in the case of Quebec at least there is no regulation of rates for interprovincial trucking.
It seems to me the railways have no place in the discussion of those rates, any more than the truckers have a place in the discussion of rates to be charged by the railways. They have never had any such right under the Transport Act or under the Railway Act; and those who are now arguing for it are saying in effect, "We will allow the truckers to come in to complain against the rates to be charged by the rail carriers on the agreed charges," whereas the railways have neither the right nor the opportunity to complain as to the rates charged by the motor vehicle operator who is attempting to get business in the two points between which he operates. We all know it is a very simple matter for a truck operator to telephone a client or a prospective client and ask him whether he will ship all his goods through him or part of his goods through him between Montreal and Toronto, for example. There is nothing to stop those two people from concluding an arrangement over the telephone. I am not suggesting that the railways should be allowed to do the same thing. I am suggesting that the railways should be allowed to compete on more even terms. I am not asking for a preference for the railways, nor am I asking for a preference for the truckers.
It has been suggested that the truckers should have the right to complain. The suggestions have been in one of two forms; first, that the individual trucker should be permitted to complain, which I understand was the suggestion made by the hon. member for Prince Albert, while the hon. member for

Transport Act
Vancouver-Quadra suggested that an association of truckers should be allowed to complain. But when you examine the provisions of subclause 1 of clause 33 you find that the ground of complaint is that the agreed charge places the business of the complainant at an unfair disadvantage. Well, now, in actual practice, as it was perfectly clear from the evidence given before the standing committee, every trucker feels that he should have the right to complain whenever an agreed charge is made which may have the effect of reducing his business.
While I sympathize with those who are affected by competition in this way, I am not asking for a preference for the rails over the trucks; I am asking for something approaching equality for the rails with the trucks. I do not feel it is proper that an individual trucker should have the right to complain against an agreed charge on the ground that he is going to lose some of his business.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: I did not suggest the individual trucker should have the right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
But the hon. member for Prince Albert made a suggestion which I interpreted in that sense. Perhaps I may have misunderstood what he said. But I do not think it is important whether it was the individual trucker or the association, for the reason that the association itself is not in business. Surely the association must come back again to the individual. With all respect for those who propose changes of that kind, I realize you would have to bring it down to an individual basis, just as we do in subclause 1, where we say:
-that the agreed charge is unjustly discriminatory against it or places its business at an unfair disadvantage.
Well, we cannot deal with the problem of the trucker on an individual basis. It was clear from the evidence before the committee that complaints would be of one of two kinds: either because some business was lost or because the shipper had agreed with the railway to give the railway what the trucker would regard as an unsatisfactory percentage of the shipper's business. In other words, where a shipper or a group of shippers and the rails agreed that the agreed charge should affect 85 per cent of the shipper's business, the trucker would like the right to complain that it should not be an 85 per cent figure, a figure arrived at perfectly freely by the parties concerned. He would like to be able to come in and say no, this should be only 65 per cent, or it should be a lower percentage, or none at all.
I do not believe it would be practical, Mr. Chairman, to suggest that the trucker should

have the right to complain against either of those aspects of the agreed charges.
I was very much concerned, after hearing the evidence and realizing the anxiety in the minds of the trucking association, that while an individual might be hurt in some specific case, there might develop a situation which could constitute a threat to the existence of the trucking industry operating between two specific points. As I said in committee, no one wants to see the elimination of any mode of transport. There is no question at all that every mode of transport we have serves a useful purpose in transportation in Canada, and we should be very hesitant about doing something which would have the effect of extinguishing any form in particular. I say that, being as much interested in the preservation of trucking as an industry as I am in seeing that the railways get a fair break.
During the course of this session we have heard many questions and comments with regard to the lay-offs of employees of the Canadian National Railways and, it might also be added, of the Canadian Pacific. We can build up employment in the railroads only if there is more traffic to carry. While I am not trying to give more traffic to the railways by this bill, yet I am trying to give them, if I may use the words of the hon. member for Prince Albert, an equal opportunity for the market that is available; in other words, to give everybody a chance to compete for the business that is there to be carried.
No one would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the trucking industry should disappear. In fact the evidence given before the royal commission demonstrated that the rather pessimistic forecasts that have been made in the past have not been realized. In 1937, when it was first proposed to introduce legislation concerning agreed charges, the trucking industry said they were about to be wiped out. The same thing was again said in 1938, I believe. When the royal commission on transportation was held in 1950-51 much the same thing was said. Then in the latter half of 1954, when Mr. Justice Turgeon presided over the commission on agreed charges, the same thing was said again, that the trucking industry was menaced with extinction.
But when one looks at the figures and finds that in 1953 there were some 824,159 motor trucks in operation as contrasted with some 220,000 in 1938, one would have to admit quite honestly that agreed charges have not put the truckers out of business. Everyone who stops and reflects for a moment will realize that the trucking industry is going to survive even under the most intensive competition from the rails.

In the brief which the truckers' association presented to the committee they referred to a questionnaire which had been sent out by the association of the United States railroads. The shippers were asked by them to state the primary reasons for their use of common, contract, and private trucking services. The information the questionnaire elicited was very interesting. This is to be found on page 36 of the typewritten brief presented by the Canadian trucking association. First on inbound traffic, shorter transit time was given by 78 per cent of the shippers as their reason for using trucks. That is something I cannot believe, despite what the hon. member for Simcoe North said about the trains between Philadelphia and New York, can be overcome by the railways. I think the trucks, for a very large part of the goods to be transported, are going to have the advantage of a shorter transit time; and that if one were to take an information survey on the subject he would find in Canada that a tremendous number of those who are using trucks now will go on using them because they provide shorter transit time than rails can provide.
If I might go on quoting from the brief, lower costs were cited by 12 per cent, and a variety of other reasons, particularly less handling, less marking and packing and less loss and damage were cited by 10 per cent of the shippers. I think this quotation is sufficient to demonstrate that the truckers occupy a useful role in the transportation economy of Canada, and that it is not going to be agreed charges or competitive rates or any other form of rate competition that is going to stop the competition between the trucks and the rails. Trucks have a useful service to render which rail transportation can never give.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: The minister mentioned 800,000-odd trucks. Are those transport trucks or would that number include private and farm trucks?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I think that is the total figure, just as was the figure of 220,000 for 1938. What I think must be guarded against is the possibility of agreed charges being made which are going to have the effect of putting out of business some segment of the transportation industry. It is because I felt there was a theoretical possibility that ought to oe guarded against that I decided it would be necessary to amend the original bill to open the door wider to references of agreed charges to the board of transport commissioners. Hence the provision of clause 33 (2) which does not contain the time limit of three months to be found in subsection 1 and which enables the governor in council,
Transport Act
if he has reason to believe that an agreed charge may be undesirable in the public interest, to refer the agreed charge to the board for investigation.
It seemed to me that was a reasonable way of providing to the trucking industry that protection against what would be an unfair situation, where agreed charges were being used as an instrument for extinguishing competition rather than attempting to meet it. An amendment was proposed to the committee and accepted by it. This morning I received a letter from the president of Canadian trucking associations dated July 7, 1955, reading as follows:
Dear Mr. Marler,
On behalf of the members of Canadian trucking associations, I wish to express our appreciation for the amendment to Bill No. 449 which you introduced on Wednesday, June 29, at the hearing of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I can agree with you that the amendment went a long distance towards meeting the case submitted by CTA. Needless to say, it is most gratifying to the association to have obtained a safeguard for the over-all position of the trucking industry in the new agreed charge legislation.
Although it is only a year since you assumed the responsibilities of Minister of Transport-
I do not like to read this, as I am not soliciting free advertising.
-it is very pleasing to our key association officials, and to me personally, to note that the tension which had existed in the relationship of the trucking industry with the government has eased very considerably. This much to be desired development bespeaks the conviction of our industry that, subject to your responsibilities in regard to all forms of transportation, the trucking industry will continue to obtain from you just and equitable consideration of its problems.
I am sorry I was forced into the position of putting that on the record.
I should like to deal with another point raised by one hon. member with regard to an amendment he had suggested before the standing committee when he said, as I recall, that the board be permitted to disallow any agreed charge. I should like to say at once that the reason I could not accept such an amendment is that I think one of the essential parts of the agreed charge under the new legislation is that the parties should feel that when it has been made, except in the most unusual cases it will not be disturbed until its life has run out; that there will be no delay in bringing it into effect and once it has been made, except in the rather exceptional cases provided for in section 33, it will not be challenged during the term of its life.
If we were to accept this suggestion that the board might disallow an agreed charge at any time it would mean there would be no security for the agreed charge, and it might be called into question at any time on

Transport Act
complaint to the board or by the board's own motion. It does seem to me, and I say this quite sincerely, that clause 33 does provide adequate opportunities for the referring of an agreed charge to the board of transport commissioners if conditions exist which justify a reference of the charge to the board for investigation.
I should like to point out that the present legislation goes a good deal further than the existing legislation. First of all, previously shippers were not permitted to make any complaint to the minister. Now an association or body representative of the shippers of a locality has the right to appeal to the minister and the minister may under the conditions set forth in subsection 1 refer the complaint to the board for investigation. Then there is the broader provision in respect to the governor in council. Whenever a condition arises which in the public interest ought to be investigated, he may refer an agreed charge to the board. Under these circumstances I do not think it is reasonable to give the board the power to disallow a charge except under the rather exceptional conditions which are outlined in section 33.
The hon. member for Peace River has referred to the transport of goods between Vancouver and Dawson Creek and the lower rates that the railways are now charging. To the best of my knowledge that would not be the result of an agreed charge. I think what has taken place is that the railways have introduced what might be regarded as a competitive rate which also would be-I am speaking without having had the opportunity of verifying the details-a constructive rate in the sense that a certain mileage is not charged for because it is assumed that there is a rail line descending from Dawson Creek more directly to the south and the haul would therefore actually be much shorter.
I believe the shippers are being given the benefit of a line that is not there in fact, but which is assumed to be there for the purpose of setting the rate. I am sure it is not under an agreed charge; it may be under a competitive rate. I can only say to the hon. member for Peace River that if it is under a competitive rate, section 334 of the Railway Act requires the rate to be compensatory. If his friends believe that it is non-compensatory they have recourse under section 334 of the act. At all events the situation of which the hon. member complains is not that people are paying more, but rather that they are paying less than they ought to pay. It is interesting to hear of a complaint that the railroads are not charging enough, so that in that respect the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River are quite unusual.

speechtext:
That would apply in the case of the areas served by the lower rates, but I am referring to people in an adjoining area.
I think the minister will admit that those people have a just complaint when they can ship through to Dawson Creek at the $1.50 per hundredweight rate, then have the goods trucked back 90 miles and still save 59 cents over the old $2.44 rate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
It sounds to me like the situation which would develop under a competitive rate established between two points where competition exists. The points between which competition does not exist would not get the benefit of the competitive rate.
Then there was the case an hon. member cited earlier with reference to Edmonton and Calgary. That was not a matter of agreed charges; it had to do with the contention of the province of Alberta that the one and one-third rule should also apply to agreed charges. That was the subject of the reference to the royal commission. I hope I have dealt adequately with the various points raised by hon. members.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: Could the minister explain just how he envisages the working out of an application under section 33 (2)? That is where someone has to complain to the governor in council.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
The sort of example I might select would be if in the making of agreed charges the railroads developed a practice of including in the agreed charges something that might be regarded as discriminatory against some other form of transport. Let us take an example that is quite fresh in the minds of members of the standing committee, the case where, let us say, without admitting it bears any relation to reality, the railways stipulate in their agreed charge that if the traffic is to be carried overseas it must go over a particular shipping line. If that were brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport, I think he would feel that it was a case in which that kind of agreed charge ought to be referred to the board for investigation, because it seems to me that is of a discriminatory character, against which no one seemingly would have the right to complain under subsection 1, and it would be a case in which the agreed charge ought to be investigated.
The truckers might reasonably be able to present facts to show that if the agreed charges put into effect between two points in Canada were pursued and continued, the extinction of the trucking industry would be inevitable. I take it that if such a case were made out to the satisfaction of the minister,

he would perhaps be able to persuade the governor in council that the agreed charges ought to be referred to the board of transport commissioners for investigation. I take it one of the things that would happen would be that the board would examine the question of whether or not the rates charged by the railways were compensatory or not.
I take it the board would then be faced with the question of deciding what ought to be done if the rates were truly compensatory and the truckers were complaining that the service was being provided at a lower cost, seemingly, than the rate at which they wished to do business themselves. I think those are two good examples in which a reference could be made.

speechtext: The application would have to be made through the Minister of Transport?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: The act does not say so, but I think that might be inferred from it.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the minister's argument against the truckers having a right to complain in this matter. subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Peace River drew to the minister's attention the freight rate change from Dawson Creek to Vancouver from $2.44 to $1.50, which the minister said was not an agreed charge. There is a question that does arise normally. The minister said the rail rate under an agreed charge must be compensatory-and "compensatory" means that the freight must not be hauled for less than cost. Last year there was a loss, which means that the freight rate should have been increased; yet we find it being decreased from $2.44 to $1.50 a hundredweight. How can you lose money and reduce the rate, and then say that the rail rates now being charged would be compensatory in a case such as that, if it were an agreed charge?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: In reply to that question I think I should say that if the rate of $2.44 does not get the business, then probably it is more profitable for the railway to be carrying the business at, let us say, $1.50 than it is to be not getting it at $2.44.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: Let us go a step further and say that the Canadian National lost $28 million last year. If that is so the rates could not be compensatory. If any rate is below the rates we have today I just do not see how you could say it is compensatory, because compensatory means you are going to carry the traffic at a profit above cost. We had to subsidize the railway last year to the extent of $28 million, so how do the rates become compensatory?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext: They can be compensatory and the railway can still lose money because of the burden of fixed charges. I think if my hon. friend would read the provision of the Railway Act, he would see it relates to the effect on the net revenue of the company, which does not mean to say it adds to the net profit.

speechtext:
the second reading of and concurrence in an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 260, to amend the Radio Act.
5S62

Radio Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RADIO ANTENNAE AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: I take it the minister is going to make some statement in explanation of the amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RADIO ANTENNAE AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have no objection to making it now but I thought of making it when the bill was in committee. If the hon. member would like me to make it now, I shall do so.
As I explained when this bill was first introduced and again on second reading, one of the changes in the Radio Act to be effected by this bill was that provided for in clause 2, which deals with the privacy of radio communications. This clause provided for the addition to section 8 of a new subsection 2 making it an offence for a person who becomes acquainted with any radio communication not intended for public use or information to make use of such communication or divulge it to any person, except when lawfully authorized to do so.
I am informed that when the bill was considered in a committee of the other place it was suggested that the proposed subsection did not make it clear how a person was to know whether a communication was intended for public use or information; and that it did not specify who was empowered to authorize or direct a person to divulge such a communication, nor did it place any limitations on that power.
In consequence the bill was, with my knowledge and concurrence, amended in the other place and a new clause 2 inserted in place of that passed by this house. The new clause would add to section 8 of the Radio Act a new subsection 2 making it an offence for a person who becomes acquainted with a radio communication transmitted otherwise than by a broadcasting station, to make use of it or divulge it except as provided in the regulations made under the Radio Act or the Canada Shipping Act, which already contain provisions to protect privacy of communications.
The new clause will not come into force until a day to be fixed by proclamation. This new clause makes it clear that there is no restriction on the use or divulging of information transmitted by broadcasting stations, but all other transmissions are to be treated as private communications except as provided in the regulations.
Before this clause is proclaimed I shall amend the general radio regulations under the authority of the Radio Act and the ship station radio regulations under the authority of the Canada Shipping Act, so as to except from the prohibition of this clause transmissions such as those containing weather information for ships and aircraft, and distress, urgency and safety messages. In addition

the regulations will specify the conditions under which a person may be authorized or required to divulge information. Such authority to divulge might be desirable, for instance, in the case of a formal inquiry in connection with a shipping casualty or an aircraft accident, or in the case of a prosecution under the Radio Act for the operation of an unlicensed station.
I believe the new clause is an improvement over that first proposal, and I commend it to this house. It does seem to me to be desirable if signals broadcast by what we regard as broadcasting stations are regarded as public communications, and if the secrecy provision is restricted to those stations which do not fall into that class. I think hon. members will appreciate the desirability of enabling communications to be transmitted over the air as to which the provisions of secrecy should apply, and that we should make it as difficult as possible for people not listening on the ordinary broadcast bands either to make use of or divulge messages that are obviously intended for private sources.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RADIO ANTENNAE AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As the
amendment with which the house is now dealing was proposed by the Senate our procedure does not make any provision for resolving the house into committee of the whole to consider it. I feel it would be much more satisfactory in a situation like this if the house could resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider such an amendment. I am satisfied that there are some aspects of this amendment, and some questions arising out of it, which could be more appropriately dealt with under the freer procedure permitted in the committee.
The minister has indicated that the Senate amendment was made with his concurrence, and he considers the result to be an improvement over clause 2 as it originally appeared in Bill No. 260. There is one question that arises immediately before I come to one of the other difficulties. The stated purpose of clause 2 of Bill No. 260 being to implement the obligations assumed by Canada under the international telecommunications convention with respect to the provision of secrecy for radio communications, I naturally ask if the clause in its amended form will accomplish the same purpose in the view of the law officers of the crown and will conform with the obligation assumed by Canada in the international telecommunications convention.
I turn from that to another aspect of the subject. The purpose of clause 2 of the bill was, as I stated, to define unlawful interception of radio communications, and having

created an offence out of such unlawful interception to attach a penalty to the offence. In the Senate amendment we have a rather different approach to the problem. Provision is made at the outset for certain exceptions, but then it is provided that subject to these exceptions, two in number-
. . . every person who, having become acquainted with any radio communication-
Then the next seven words are new:
-transmitted otherwise than by a broadcasting station, makes use of such communication or divulges it to any person is guilty of an offence . . .
Then the penalties are set out. The new words relate to the two exceptions at the outset and then to the definition of radio communication, "transmitted otherwise than by a broadcasting station." I do not think there is any far-reaching difficulty arising out of the words "transmitted otherwise than by a broadcasting station", although the expression is very broad. There are two exceptions laid down in the opening words of the clause as amended. The first involves a class of exceptions to be created by the minister under the power given to him to make regulations under the act, and the second arises under regulations made under the Canada Shipping Act.
The minister has indicated to the house he is prepared to make regulations excepting from the provisions of this new clause of the act communications about weather for ships and aircraft, communications relating to safety and communications relating to casualties. It is a little difficult in this brief discussion now to know how far he is prepared to go in that respect. There is always a problem, it seems to me, as to the proper function of regulations in a matter of this kind. Here you have a general provision in the legislation providing that those who become acquainted with any radio communication transmitted otherwise than by a broadcasting station and who make use of it or divulge it are guilty of an offence, subject to exceptions to be made by the minister in the form of regulations.
It seems to me that is not a very satisfactory way to proceed by legislation, to give the minister power to create exceptions to what is otherwise a general rule laid down by statute. The minister may have a perfectly good intent with regard to the kind of exceptions he proposes to create under this regulatory power, but I am very doubtful if it is a proper use to make of regulatory power, or if the house ought to pass legislation which gives the minister power to write exceptions to the general rule laid down in the statute law itself.

No one else in the house knows at the moment and perhaps the minister himself does not even know, how far he proposes to go in excepting from the general language of the section communications in relation to casualties, for instance. I do not know whether the minister is aware of it, but there is a situation involved here in which, if we pass the legislation in the form in which it has come from the Senate, it seems to me we are likely to create serious difficulty. I am referring now to the practice of newspapers, particularly in the urban centres, having their own receiving stations and having them tuned in on the shortwave transmitting facilities of both the provincial and local police. This is a very general practice in the urban centres. Indeed, I believe in the case of practically all the big daily newspapers they have special shortwave radio receivers which are tuned in on the shortwave transmitting facilities of both the provincial police and the urban police. I know the three big daily newspapers in Toronto all have facilities for tuning in on the provincial police transmitter located at Aurora, just a few miles north of Toronto.
A reporter in each of these newspaper offices is detailed to listen to the receiver. To the great majority of the messages that come over it, perhaps even 90 per cent of them, he perhaps pays no attention, but in the case of accidents on the highways it is by this means that the newspapers receive their information. If word of an accident comes over the receiver it is then within the power of the newspaper to direct a local correspondent, if there is one in the area of the accident, to go to the scene if the accident is sufficiently important or serious; or if the accident happens close enough to the newspaper office and is serious enough it may be that a reporter or photographer will be sent to the scene.
The same applies to the shortwave facilities used by the municipal police. Indeed, at municipal police headquarters in Toronto I am told there is a small press room containing a receiver tuned in to the city police wavelength, and each of the newspapers maintains a reporter in that press room whose main if not sole duty it is to listen to the police calls. Formerly the receiver picked up only messages given to the police cars by the police dispatcher, but at the request of the newspapers the set was altered so it also receives reports from the police cars to the dispatcher. The police not only tolerate the listening in by the newspapers but fully co-operate to ensure that the newspapers are adequately informed.
It seems to me that the amendment we are now asked to approve is going to make

Radio Act
it an offence for newspapers to listen in on the transmission of these oftentimes important messages from the police. Let it not be thought that there is any danger of abuse here. Some may say, what about raids? Is it right that messages of that kind should go to the newspapers? The fact is that messages concerning raids are not sent out by the police over the shortwave facilities. Similarly, what about reports of arrests? The fact is that reports of arrests are not broadcast in this manner either.
I do not know whether this point has been brought to the attention of the minister previously or whether, if it has, it is the sort of matter he proposes to except from the provisions of the act under the power given to him by the amendment to pass regulations for the purposes of creating exemptions. But I am quite certain that the house does not wish to pass legislation the effect of which would be to make it an offence punishable by both fine and imprisonment for a newspaper to listen in with their approval to the shortwave messages sent out by both the provincial and municipal police authorities.
I mentioned earlier that the procedure we are bound to follow when we are dealing with a Senate amendment does not permit us to resolve the house into committee, where we might have some further opportunity of a more informal discussion than is permitted by the procedure in the house. However, may I call it six o'clock and ask the minister, if he has not already concerned himself with this point, to give it consideration and perhaps say something to me about it later.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I might reply at once to the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor) I would say that as I understand the law at present, radio amateurs are obliged to subscribe to a declaration of secrecy. I do not think they are specially affected by the legislation now under consideration. I believe they are bound to a much greater degree than are others in connection with making use or divulging of information they are able to obtain.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) raised this afternoon an interesting point with regard to the secrecy of police calls. I would point out to the house in connection with police calls that some municipalities have already made complaints to my department against the use of shortwave receivers which enable individuals to intercept police calls, because these municipalities regard such calls as intended for the benefit of the members of the police force. They have actually submitted cases to the department in which it was quite obvious that the information transmitted by the police radio system had been misused.
On the other hand, as the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out this afternoon, there are police departments in other cities which are perfectly agreeable to police calls being intercepted by receivers installed in offices of local newspapers and in some instances, I am told, by photographers.
There is no intention on the part of my department to interfere with an established practice of this kind. I have made inquiries from those who administer the radio licensing regulations, and I am told that it is the standard practice where a wavelength is allotted to some licensee for the purpose of transmitting messages, to issue commercial receiving station licences to those who are to receive the calls. For instance, in the case of a police department, each of the cars would be licensed to receive the signals sent out by the police department radio.
Therefore we would have in mind in administering the proposed legislation that where police departments have no objection to newspapers or others receiving their particular signals, we would issue commercial receiving station licences to those newspapers and others, if the police department in question had no objection to such licences being issued. And, as I had an opportunity of saying to the hon. member for Eglinton during the dinner recess, there would be no reason why a licence should not be issued if for example a newspaper office wished to be
Radio Act
licensed to receive calls, we will say, from (he provincial or local police, or the fire department, if none of these transmitters had any objection. Under these circumstances we would be prepared to issue the licence and enable the licensee to receive calls from all three sources, provided they did not object. I might add for the information of the house, Mr. Speaker, that the licence fee is a nominal amount. I am told that at the present time it is $2.
I should also like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the same views would prevail with regard to calls from municipal fire departments. If there is no objection to newspaper officers being licensed to receive those calls, the department itself would have no reason to object. In essence, those who are effecting the transmission are in a position to say whether they wish it to be public or private; and when they say they have no objection to the newspapers listening in, it is quite obvious they regard them as public.
There are two other points I should like to deal with. One is the question of whether the bill as amended would implement our undertakings under the international telecommunications convention and the regulations made under it. I understand our legal advisers are satisfied that the bill would accomplish this purpose.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Eglinton expressed the view that it would be more desirable to proceed by setting forth in the bill the cases in which the secrecy provisions were to apply rather than to proceed by way of exception, as the amendment does. I would say, Mr. Speaker, it would be preferable if we could in some simple way follow that process. But I may say that when the subject was examined-and it was examined very carefully-it was found that it was not possible or practical to proceed in that way, and it was necessary to provide that we should proceed by way of exception rather than by a principal provision which would define exactly the body of people to whom the secrecy provisions were intended to apply.
It may be that after we have had some experience with the legislation we shall be able to find some simpler language than that now used in the amendment, but all I can say for the present is that we shall endeavour to administer the legislation, if it passes, in such a way as not to create difficulties where difficulties ought not to be created, and not to impose secrecy restrictions where they will be merely a handicap and a hardship on those who would be listening to the messages with which we are dealing

In Alberta you made a reasonable compromise.

That was a different situation. We do not want to go over each one of these in detail. Every effort was made to meet conditions without departing, if possible, from the general set-up of the reorganization. In these two particular instances, the two battalions were created and they each carry the name of one of the old battalions as a secondary name. The North Nova Scotia Highlanders became the 1st battalion, Nova Scotia Highlanders North. The other unit from Cape Breton became the 2nd battalion, Nova Scotia Highlanders Cape Breton. The idea of having one tartan in Nova Scotia was simply that in time of war it would lead to a minimum of confusion and difficulty and make the personnel interchangeable if that should become necessary. So far as I know, it was left to the local units to decide on a tartan. Unfortunately I do not think they have decided on that, at least it has not been reported to me.
Yes, they did.

If so it has not been reported to me.
I want to reiterate to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert what I said to the hon. member who preceded him. Since the estimates were before the committee on June 30, I have looked into the matter and the first telegrams and letters were received in late August or early September. In each case, however, the matter was carried forward principally at the local level with the local officials, and only came to me later.

All I can say is that what the minister has just said bears out the tribute I paid to him a little while ago about the adroit and easy way in which he deals with these matters we raise. The minister says it is true that this has only happened in three places, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The fact is he has had protests from two out of three, so I do not think his batting average is too good on that.
He also told us a moment ago that he thought no arrangement had been made with respect to the plaid. As I pointed out the other night-and this is the gravamen of my complaint-you have the North Nova Scotia Highlanders and the Pictou County Highlanders agreeing as between themselves. They

are faced with a demand from the minister's department that "you have to amalgamate into one battalion; what are you going to do about it?" They come up with the proposal that they will maintain the name of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, thus perpetuating the name of a regiment which served overseas in the last war, and adopt the plaid of the Pictou County Highlanders, the Mackenzie plaid, which has an official affiliation with the Seaforth battalion. In that way they will maintain both the ancient traditions of the Seaforths and the name of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, who served overseas.
First of all they are told that is a reasonable proposal and that something can be worked out to that end. Then they are told later that it cannot be accepted, that they have to become the 1st battalion of the Nova Scotia highland regiment. They are told that if they cannot agree to adopt the Pictou County plaid they will be told what to wear, and if they do not want to accept that they can wear the old uniforms and new officers coming in will wear something else.
I am concerned with only two questions. Why did the department not at least consider the recommendation of these reserve officers and men who said, "You want two battalions; here they are. We will merge the Pictous and the North Nova Scotians into one and leave Cape Breton as it is. That gives you two battalions with their names, traditions and all the rest of it." Since that was not done I ask the minister this question. I know he has had a great deal of experience as a trial lawyer. He is used to practising expediency, he is used to compromise, and he is used to common sense. I suggest to the minister in all seriousness that if he goes through the file on this matter he will agree -he will not agree publicly and I would not expect him to-that he should tell someone that they have not used too much common sense in connection with this matter, and that he thinks some reasonable compromise can be made. If he will promise the committee now that he will consider the matter again I am prepared to leave it in his hands on his assurance he will give it consideration, because frankly I do not think he has.

I should like to say a word on this matter. As many hon. members know, the constituency of Cumberland is one from which a large number of members of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders were recruited in the last war. We in that constituency have a very dear feeling for the name and the fame of that unit. I have been reading only recently a book by our eminent 50433-378J
Supply-National Defence Nova Scotia author, Dr. Will R. Bird, entitled "No Retreating Footsteps". That is an ang-licization of the motto, I think you would call it, of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders.
I think that is a very proud motto. I hope to present the minister with a copy of the book eventually. I know that as a student of military history he will be very glad to receive it. But I can say with assurance that any Nova Scotian or other Canadian who reads the book will feel a very strong surge of patriotic pride when he reads the record of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders in the last war.
For that reason we have a very dear feeling so far as the regiment is concerned. The other day the hon. member for Colchester-Hants expressed the feelings of his constituents. This matter is close to our hearts, and I join with others who have spoken in asking the minister to give it the most careful and sympathetic consideration. Surely some way can be found in which more of the former identities of these highland units can be preserved. I am not a military expert. I do not presume to say that no degree of reorganization is necessary, but in the present scheme it seems to me that the former identities of these units, their battle honours and their records, are going to be submerged and are going to become dimmer as the years go by. Even if it is considered imperative that there must be only one highland regiment in Nova Scotia, it certainly seems to me some scheme can be worked out whereby the proud records and names of these units can be preserved at least to a far greater extent than is the case under the present scheme. As I say, I join with all the others in urging the minister to give the matter the most careful consideration before a final, irrevocable plan is made.

Mr. Chairman, I rise once again to join those who have spoken on this matter in the last few minutes. I do so because I had the honour of serving in the same division as the North Nova Scotia Highlanders. As the last speaker has just said, in my opinion there was no regiment in the Canadian army that served with more distinction during the last conflict than this unit. I think a regiment of that kind deserves to retain its name, its traditions, its battle honours, its tartan and everything else.
I am not so familiar with the Pictou County Highlanders, but I feel sure they have just as honourable a record as the North Nova Scotia Highlanders. I join with those who have urged that this matter be given very serious consideration, because there is nothing that can destroy a unit quicker than to take away the things the minister and his
5972	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence department are seeking to take away at the present time. I join the others in urging that these traditions, these names, these tartans, all these things that go to make a militia regiment what it is, be left as nearly intact as possible.

First of all I should like to say that I resent very much the implication the minister has left, that we cannot man our regiments in the maritimes. I do not know whether we have too many battalions and regiments for our area, but I think the minister and his officials will agree that in both the first and second world war the maritimes had the highest-I repeat, the highest- recruiting averages in Canada. I know that M.D. 7 in New Brunswick led the whole dominion in recruiting for at least three years of the second world war. It may be that is due to our economic conditions; nevertheless I want the record to be clear that we are as patriotic as any area in Canada. Therefore the implication left that the reason the department has to play around with these names is that we are short of men in our area does not hold water with me.
I remember that the Royal Rifles of Canada were short of men before they went to Hong Kong. They came down from Quebec and in the northern part of New Brunswick they found the recruits they wanted. A great many of those boys did not come back, but that is getting on a sentimental strain and I wish to be very practical and make my point. I only do so because the minister has emphasized the fact that priorities of time are a big consideration with his department.
I referred to the kilts that the New Brunswick Scottish regiment purchased last year. On the day the regiment was wiped out as a result of the Kennedy report the new kilts arrived by boat from England. I cannot vouch for the story, but it is said that when the regiment was at Camp Utopia last July and the news was received of its disbanding, one of the senior officers took off his kilt on the parade ground in front of everybody and said, "There, take it; it is no good to me any more." The whole point I am making is that these kilts had been ordered and the officers had to pay for them themselves. Yet when they actually arrived the regiment was completely wiped out. What is going to happen? Are these men going to receive any compensation because of the change that was made?
I have a very nice letter from the department, but it just stalls in the matter.
I am discussing the matter here this evening only because the minister has stressed the point of priority in time. He said we were too late. At least, after all the discussion there has been on the estimates of the


department, we have established the point that some compensation should be paid.
I received from the department a very nice letter concerning this $175 the officers had to pay for their kilts. In substance the letter said, "Wear out the kilts". Well, after all, there is not much practical use to which kilts can be put if they are not used by the enlisted men. They now have a regiment that is not kilted. I do suggest seriously that the kilts are of no value to these men now, and some compensation should be made to them.

It just struck me, Mr. Chairman, that when that officer of the New Brunswick Highlanders took off his kilt on the parade square he resolved the very ancient question which has troubled a large part of the world for many years; what does the highlander wear under his kilt? However, we do not have the word of any witness who was present to tell us what he did wear under his kilt.
However, to return more seriously to the subject under discussion, it seems to me the minister is in no difficulty so far as this matter is concerned. So far as the two highland regiments are concerned it seems to me it comes down to a decision in the matter of the tartan they are to wear. Surely the minister would have no difficulty in saying, "Well, let the Cape Breton Highlanders wear the tartan they have always worn and let the North Nova Scotia Highlanders wear the tartan which they and the other regiment have decided they will wear".
The minister said if it were decided they were to wear the same tartan there would be no difficulty in changing over from one battalion to another in war. But the minister must know that in time of war they do not wear these tartans at all; they wear battle-dress. The only people who wear tartans in time of war are members of the pipe band. Members of the pipe band of whichever battalion was organized could wear the tartan of that battalion; or they could be mixed, and there would be no difficulty. So, as I say, I do not believe the minister is in any difficulty on this matter at all. All he has to do is say, "We will let these Highland battalions wear the tartans they wish to wear".
Would the minister promise to consider this matter?
I do not wish to get too deeply involved in this battle of the tartans.
And Irishmen.

I do wish to say in my own defence, however, that I think someone might have mentioned that since I became minister I have put the highland militia units in kilts.

So far as the point at issue is concerned, most certainly I shall review it. I was impressed by the arguments concerning the situation as it exists, and I do not wish anyone to think that I am being stubborn about it. Because of the eloquent remarks addressed to me on behalf of highland regiments I shall certainly take another look at the situation. I am not making any promise as to the result, but I will look into it.

There are one or two other points I wish to mention in connection with the militia. The first of these concerns another highland regiment, the Calgary Highlanders. The point I have in mind is in connection with military bands. The matter came up in Calgary last fall, when the commanding officer of the Calgary Highlanders gave his permission for the pipe band of that regiment to play at the Calgary Stam-peders' football game. I understand members of the band were delighted with the prospect of playing. Arrangements went forward, and they were to provide the entertainment by countermarching and piping during the intermission of the rugby game. However, not long before the day of the game the musicians' union from its headquarters in Toronto, I think, sent out an order forbidding the band to appear at the game.
This raises the entire question of just who is going to control military bands. Is it going to be the commanding officer of the regiment, who is supposed to have control of the personnel under his command, or is it to be the United States boss of a labour union-and essentially in this case it goes back to Petrillo in the United States-who is to say when and where military bands will be permitted to play?
Since this affair in Calgary there have been many arguments and heartburnings. I should add that the Department of National Defence has been quite wishy-washy in the matter. It seems to me that the department -and I am referring particularly to the minister-should come out forthwith and say that the commanding officer of a regiment having a military band shall have the final say as to when and where the band shall play. If, because they belong to the musicians' union or for some other reason, the members of the band do not wish to continue, that is another matter. They, as individuals, are at perfect liberty to decide. But for one of our military bands forming part of the Canadian militia, part of a unit in the Canadian army, to be placed in a position where after being ordered by the commanding officer to go on parade it finds that the order is countermanded by the head of a union in the United States, is not to be tolerated.
Supply-National Defence
The time has come to put an end to that situation, and to place the commanding officer of each militia regiment in a position where he can say to his band that, if circumstances warrant and the men are agreeable, the band may play here or may play there or many play some other place, without having to take dictation from across the border, from the head of any labour union over there.

I would like to add my support to what has been said by the hon. member for Calgary North. No union, or no head of any union, should have anything to say regarding the orders to be handed out to our army, our navy or our flying force. Anything like that is absolutely ridiculous. Regimental bands have refused to play in Canada simply because some foreign dictator in a union has dared to say they cannot play. Now is the time to stop all that nonsense. They have no right and no place at any time in any of the armed forces of the Dominion of Canada that serve Her Majesty. She comes above them all, and so do her commanding officers.
Now is the time for the minister to say that there shall be no more dictation by any local union, or by any foreign union, or any other kind of union in any part of Her Majesty's forces. That sort of thing should be done away with.
Without working up any undue heat in this matter-
That is a matter of opinion.
Well, I was not really referring to the hon. member for Simcoe North. I wonder whether the minister could spell out definitely what is the position so far as military bands are concerned?

Mr. Chairman, I understand this is an issue of long standing, and various methods have been evolved in an endeavour to meet it. But the situation as it exists now is that a militia band can be ordered out by the commanding officer on any military parade or to attend any military function, and it should and does perform its function on those occasions. But if a militia band is required for some other purpose than military duties, such as the case the hon. member mentioned, a stampede or any civilian function, then the rule is that it must have the consent of the local union which would otherwise supply the band.
In that connection I might point out that most of the members of the militia bands are also members of unions, and unless they kept peace with their union we would not

Supply-National Defence have them long in the military band. Therefore the working arrangements in this picture are pretty well known now, and we try to use our bands to the best advantage of the public at various functions. But one of the prerequisites, other than a military function, is that they must have the consent of the local union. In the short time I have been minister I have had very little difficulty with the situation. It is a working arrangement which seems to work reasonably well.

Mr. Chairman, the case I mentioned does not come within most of the conditions the minister has just mentioned. The members of the Calgary Highlanders pipe band were quite willing and anxious to come and play on this occasion. Their commanding officer had made arrangements for them to come and play, and was also anxious to have them play. In spite of that fact the musicians' union forbade them to play. As a result they were not allowed to play. I hope Senator Tom Reid is not in the gallery, but the whole question-
He is at home in British Columbia, like most of the senators.

The whole question of
whether the pipes were musical instruments was introduced into this argument, and it was put forth quite seriously in the Calgary papers that the pipes were not musical instruments and therefore the musicians' union should not have any right to dictate to this band as to where they played or did not play. It just happened that one or two members of the band, I understand, were members of the musicians' union. They were not playing pipes but were playing other instruments when they were playing in other bands. Because of the fact that two or three members of the pipe band of that regiment happened to be musicians who played string or brass instruments or something else in other bands, the whole band, in spite of the desire of the members, in spite of the desire of the commanding officer, and in spite of the desire of practically everybody in the city of Calgary, were prevented from playing. I would ask the minister whether it is not possible to prevent a situation of that sort recurring.
Did they refuse to play at a military function?

Nobody refused to play, Mr. Chairman. The band wanted to play at it. I understand the commanding officer wanted them to play at it. The musicians' union, because two or three members of that pipe band belonged to other bands where they played other instruments, refused the band
[Mr. Campney.l
permission to play. As a result it was not allowed to play. As a matter of fact it was not allowed to play on orders of the minister or the officials of his department. The matter was referred immediately to national defence headquarters, and the order came back from the minister, or from some responsible official of his department, that the band must not play.

It was not a military function. I thought I made that clear. As far as getting involved in an argument about pipes is concerned, I just had a discussion about highland regiments. I do not want to now get into an argument with the hon. member about pipes. I thought I had made the distinction clear between military functions and civilian functions.

Mr. Chairman, it was not a military function. That was never in question. But the members of the pipe band wanted to play at the function. The commanding officer of the regiment wanted them to play at the function, and I would say at least 95 per cent of the people of Calgary wanted them to play at the function. They were prevented from playing at the function by the musicians' union on dictation from some union headquarters in the United States, because two or three members of the band happened to be members of other bands where they played different instruments. It makes a completely ridiculous situation which the minister by militia orders-that is all that is required-should take steps to see does not recur.

I have listened to this discussion on military bands. I should just like to say it would appear that international co-operation out in western Canada is not as good as it is in eastern Canada, or that part of the country from which I come. Just one week ago today I attended an international gathering in Eastport, Maine, which is in the United States. There were two boats of the Canadian navy and one boat of the United States navy lying side by side in that United States harbour. The lieutenant governor of our province, members of our provincial legislature and others were in attendance. That Sunday night, which would be a week ago last night, the citizens of the city of Eastport heard one of the finest concerts ever heard in that city, and it was played by a band from a Canadian ship. I saw the parade in which they took part, and I can assure you that they did a very fine job. If the lack of co-operation which has been exemplified here tonight does really exist in western Canada, I assure you it cannot be found on the Atlantic coast line.

I might say to the hon. member for Charlotte, who has been talking about lack of co-operation with respect to bands or anything else in western Canada that he just does not know what he is talking about. I would tell him, Mr. Chairman, that about 10 hours ago more United States bands than he has ever seen in Canada marched down the streets of Calgary in the Calgary Stampede parade. That happened about 10 hours ago, this very day. The co-operation between our people in western Canada and the people of the United States, as far as bands are concerned and otherwise, is a great deal better than anything the hon. member for Charlotte knows in his part of the country.
But that is a complete red herring. It has absolutely nothing to do with the point I raised as to who is going to control military bands, and particularly pipe bands.
I am sorry to say the minister is still taking the position which I am afraid he took last fall in connection with this matter when the thing came up, namely a wishy-washy attitude. I thought probably the minister by this time would have said a military band is under the command of the commanding officer of the regiment, and that where the commanding officer of the regiment orders it to play, so long as the members of that band are satisfied that they should play there, there shall be no question of what Mr. Caesar Petrillo, of the musicians' union, wants or anything of that sort. I would hope that would still be the minister's attitude.
I may have misunderstood the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North. I was sure I understood him to criticize the United States union for interfering with the Canadian band.
Certainly I did.

I can assure him there was no United States union that interfered with the Canadian band. I would go further and say there was no interference of any kind. They were there for three days. They played two or three band concerts and took part in two different parades. There was no interference so far as any United States union was concerned. There may be one that exists out in Alberta, but there is none down on the Atlantic coast.
I want to support the hon. member for Calgary North in what he has said.
