I was going on to say I would support the minister in the power he has, that once he gives permission for a military band to play anywhere then there should be no interference. The principle involved in this is whether or not the power of the musicians' union, which is affiliated with the United States union, is going to interfere with a military band playing anywhere under any circumstances.
We found the same thing in our radio committee, though I cannot discuss that at this time. The fact is that a military band cannot play for a radio station without a standby band being there. Although that standby band does not play, it is paid. Of course that is a sort of commercial venture. I submit that too much power is being placed in the hands of the unions.
A parallel case would be where the minister wanted to use army trucks to transport something from one place to another. I know the truckers' union would not step in if the army were transporting army goods, but supposing there was a flood or some emergency of that kind and the minister instructed the army trucks to transport non-army goods from one place to another. If the truckers' union came along and said, "No, you cannot do that, would the minister retreat and say, "Well, these are not army goods so we had better call off the boys"?
If we are running an army, air force and navy for the purpose of defence and all that goes with it, then they should be under the supervision and control of the minister. Although there is quite a labour element in my riding I submit that it is possible for the labour bosses to become more powerful than even the Minister of National Defence. It will be pretty serious when that happens. A band is not going to win or lose a battle, though it might help in winning, but I think this is a serious principle and I support the hon. member for Calgary North in his contention.

We could solve the whole problem quite simply if we used military bands only for military purposes. There is never any objection or trouble where that is done. But when we try to make these bands available for civilian organizations or functions when it is convenient for the men to play it is only then that we come into conflict with the civilian bands or civilian musicians' organizations. A great many of the members of militia bands are also members of a union and make their living or part of their living by playing in civilian bands. If we were to say, irrespective of whether it was a military function or not, that we were going out into the musical world to compete with
5976	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence civilian bands, we would come into conflict, not only with civilian organizations organized for that purpose but we would jeopardize the future in their union of the men in the militia band who belonged to the union. Very soon we would not have any militia bands, which perhaps would be another way of solving the problem.
I should like to make it clear that there is a definite distinction. I think the analogy of the hon. member for Macleod about truck drivers is not relevant, as there is no difficulty at all when the function is military in character. It is only when out of the goodness of our hearts we make military bands available for civilian functions that we must obtain the consent of the union in that locality.
This has been established for some time; it is not my idea. I understand that it works better now than when there was no such arrangement, when there was always trouble. I think our disposition of the matter is reasonable and fair and effective.

All I can say is that 95 per cent, if not more, of the people of Calgary do not think it is fair and reasonable. I know that the members of the Calgary Highlanders who are especially concerned think it is extraordinarily unreasonable that this situation should prevail. The minister says it is only when these bands go out in competition with other bands that there is any trouble, but I would ask the minister, in what way could a military highland pipe band compete with members of a musicians' union?
That is a question I do not feel called upon to answer.

I think the minister does not feel called upon to answer because there is no answer. They just do not compete, that is ail there is to it. To deny the use of this pipe band for civic functions is an example of dictation by the musicians' union headquarters in the United States which is completely unbearable as far as Canada and the Canadian army are concerned, and something which should be ended immediately.
The Department of National Defence is spending thousands of dollars every day advertising for recruits in our newspapers. What better recruiting agency could you have than a good military band?

I have a few questions I should like to ask the minister on a totally different subject. During the course of his remarks when this debate was initiated or in the white paper, I am not sure which, he said that as far as the reserve forces are concerned the anti-tank role which was formerly performed by anti-tank artillery regiments had


been taken over by the armoured corps. I should like to know what armoured corps regiments have been specifically defined for this anti-tank job and also what those regiments are armed with, though they may not be armed at this stage because the transition took place only in the last few months.
I understand that there are 22 armoured regiments, and they are training with Sherman tanks.
The minister says there are 22 armoured regiments which have been designated for anti-tank duties specifically. How many armoured regiments are there altogether in the reserve?
There are 22 armoured regiments.

That is the answer I anticipated, that there were only 22 armoured regiments in the reserve. What the minister has told us is that all the armoured regiments have now been designated for antitank defence. Therefore I would like to ask him where the armour for the Canadian army, if we have to mobilize, is going to come from. We have two regular force armoured regiments, and that is all. I think it is quite apparent that if we had to mobilize for a general war we would have to have a considerable number of armoured regiments. If all the reserve force regiments were designated anti-tank regiments, formerly artillery regiments, where is our armour going to come from?

I understand the same organization and the same equipment obtains, whether they are armoured regiments in an armoured brigade or whether they are for service with infantry divisions. The same equipment and the same organization obtains in each case.

Mr. Chairman, I would understand from this answer that actually, instead of there being 22 armoured regiments designated for anti-tank defence, there are no regiments of any kind designated for antitank defence. When the artillery regiments were wiped out in the recent reorganization, the anti-tank role really disappeared.
Having spent some five years during the war chiefly as an anti-tank gunner, I can tell the minister with some authority that a regiment trained as a tank regiment is not an anti-tank regiment and will not and cannot be effective as an anti-tank regiment. As a result of that experience I would ask the minister what special training, if any, in the anti-tank role these armoured regiments are receiving.
I understand that the training, the organization and the equipment are the same in each case. At least these regiments get the training that fits them for either activity.

Mr. Chairman, I happen to have a certain amount of familiarity with two armoured regiments, and to my knowledge they have had no training whatever in an anti-tank role. They have been trained as tank regiments, and that is the only training they have received. As I indicated earlier, training in an anti-tank role is on a completely different basis from training as a tank regiment. I know this to my own extreme cost and, as a matter of fact, to the cost to this country of a considerable number of self-propelled anti-tank 17-pounders which I was forced to use as tanks during the advance to Breda, through Breda to Bergen op Zoom and through Bergen op Zoom. We lost a considerable amount of armour there owing to the fact that anti-tank trained troops were forced to use anti-tank weapons as tanks. Similarly when we tried to use tanks in the role of anti-tank weapons they failed, because they had not been trained in that role.
When the minister tells me that 22 armoured regiments in the Canadian militia are interchangeable as anti-tank regiments or as tank regiments, I would say that he has been misinformed by his advisers. Otherwise, if his advisers have not told him that, he does not know what the situation is, because he has no experience in the matter. If his advisers have told him that, I would say he has been very badly misinformed. I helped to bury many men who would prove that information was incorrect.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there anything further under militia?

I should like to have an answer from the minister as to whether there are any regiments which will be specifically trained in an anti-tank role, which was one of the most important roles in any army during the last war.
My officials tell me, as I said a moment ago, that all of them will be trained in each of the two roles. I cannot make it any clearer. The intention is that each of them will be trained in each role.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I
should like to make this observation. I do not believe it is possible to train a regiment in both roles sufficiently and effectively, from the experience not only of myself but of a very large number of people in the last war. I think the minister should change his concept.
Supply-National Defence Certain regiments should be definitely designated for anti-tank defence and trained for that, and the remainder of the regiments should continue as they have been up to the present time, as tank regiments. A tank regiment is essentially an offensive formation, trained on the basis of attacking. An antitank regiment is the exact reverse. It is organized and trained on the basis of defending against tank attack. To expect one regiment to be completely and reasonably trained as far as both ends of this are concerned just will not work. As I say, on the basis of practical experience I am quite certain it will not work.
There is one other matter, Mr. Chairman, and that is in connection with ack-ack regiments. Possibly you might have divined by this time that I am a gunner. I should like to ask the minister how many ack-ack regiments are left in the militia; how many of those are light ack-ack, and how many heavy ack-ack?
There are eight light ack-ack regiments and nine heavy ack-ack regiments.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister what the armament of the nine heavy ack-ack regiments is, and if there is any plan to equip these regiments with rockets or any other form, whatever the name may be, of ground to air weapons of the rocket type?
The heavy anti-aircraft are equipped with 3-7.
The same weapon as we had in the last war?

Yes. There are 90 mm. guns in stock, but the militia regiments have not been re-equipped with them.
As to the question about guided missiles, all I can say about that is that very intensive studies are being made with respect to guided missiles but they have not made the progress as to practical use that we might have hoped. We are studying various types, and those studies will continue until we determine what seems to be a proper and useful solution for Canada.

I believe it would be a good thing for the morale of the light ack-ack and heavy ack-ack regiments, particularly, if there were some reasonable degree of expectation they might be equipped with modern ack-ack defence weapons. I understand that some of the national guard units in the United States, which correspond to our militia units, have been equipped with some of these ground to air missiles. I believe you can understand, Mr. Chairman, that it is rather discouraging for the ack-ack gunners of this country to look

Supply-National Defence across the border and see their counterparts have these rocket weapons of various sorts while they are still using the weapon which was the standard weapon in the last war. I believe the minister himself, or the previous minister, has stated in this house on numerous occasions that that weapon is obsolescent.
So far as the general morale of these ack-ack regiments is concerned, I would hope the minister might be able to make an early announcement that some of them at least are going to be provided with a few of these rocket type weapons. This would enable them to carry on their activities with some idea that they are going to be reasonably up to date.

I feel that the discussion of the militia would proceed in a better manner if the minister would deal with the militia in general. Unfortunately, when he was introducing his estimates on June 16 he devoted just three short paragraphs to the militia. He said then he would deal briefly with it, and that is correct. That is all he did. He said the response to the reorganization had been good and had resulted in better coordination and training. There were a few sentences like that.
When we came to this particular section, it would have been wiser for the minister to have outlined the general situation in so far as the militia is concerned. I would suggest to him that another year that might very well be done. For example, well over a year ago I believe a report was submitted to the department concerning the reorganization of the militia. No information was given to this house, nor so far as I know was made public before the house rose at the end of June last year.
Even now we have not a general picture of the militia. Questions have been raised and were raised again on June 30 concerning certain items with regard to the militia. The general picture is not in the possession of the house. I think the minister should inform us with regard to the general strength of the militia on paper and the actual strength; the composition of the militia broken down according to the various corps, infantry, artillery and so on. I think he should be able to tell us now-we are well into July-the number of militia units training at camp and the total personnel present.
I feel the minister might very well put on the record the general reorganization of the militia that was to take place according to the Kennedy report. It may be that only certain of the recommendations in that report have been incorporated in the militia. There may be others that are coming forward during the
[Mr. Harkness.l

course of this year or later. With that information in the possession of the house I feel our discussion of the militia would proceed along more regular lines.
I would suggest to the minister, too, if he will comment on this, that when the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich was speaking he drew attention to the value there would be in the future to giving special training in civil defence to the militia. Perhaps that was considered by the committee reporting on the reorganization of the militia. As it stands at the moment, we have no picture in front of us as to the militia, and I feel it would be helpful if the minister would undertake to give us that picture.

With regard to the background of the organization of the militia, Mr. Chairman, the subject was exhaustively dealt with by my predecessor in the house on June 21, 1954, at which time he enumerated all the steps that were being taken. On pages 7 and 8 of the white paper there are five or six paragraphs setting out in general terms what has been done. Then there is a figure showing the strength of the militia as of December 31 last on page 23 of the white paper. I am told that the total effective strength of the militia as of April 20 of this year was 45,828.
While we cannot yet give an exact return of the number who will attend camp this year, estimates are that there will be 19,000, which is substantially more than last year. I did receive today a report from two of our senior officers who have been visiting the training camps. They expressed themselves as very gratified with what they saw, and said that the militia units are taking full advantage of the time available to them for training. Many of the commanding officers expressed the opinion that the numbers, which are greater this year, would be increased in future years. They believe the steps taken in bringing about a reorganization have produced substantial results.

I should like to ask the minister if he can give us some idea of the arrangement at national headquarters with respect to the training and organization of the militia. What general provision is there for the allocation of duties to officers of the permanent forces who supervise the organization and training of the militia, and for the allocation of permanent instructors, and so on, to the militia?

General Letson is the special adviser to the chief of the general staff on militia matters and advises the chief of the general staff. With him is Colonel Buell, who is on the general staff as director of militia and cadets. These two positions

are new positions and are filled by the gentlemen I have mentioned. They in turn tie their activities into the existing organization of the department so far as the militia is concerned.
